comment_text: From: mkearns525@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 2/10/2026 8:35:23 AM Subject: Docket ID# EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 — Opposition to Proposed 2026 Changes to Circumscribe Certification Authority of States and Tribes -------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from mkearns525@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, EPA’s proposed 2026 rule changes that would circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water will have a negative effect on the environment. Clean water is critical for life for all of us and once it is polluted, it can’t be unpolluted. Congress enacted the Clean Water Act to protect, restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. The EPA’s proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. The EPA’s proposed 2026 certification rules are unlawful, unreasonable, and just plain wrong. Specifically: 1. ) I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations. 2. ) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. 3. ) I oppose all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water. 4. ) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 5. ) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish. Thank you for considering my comments, Sincerely, Ma Meg Kearns 525 Sparkman Ave Duluth, MN 55803-2149 mkearns525@gmail.com

comment_text: Board of Directors Doug Crow Ghost, SRST Chairman Reno Red Cloud, OST Vice Chairman Issabelle Provost, YST Secretary Mary J. Gourneau, LBST Treasurer Elizabeth Wakeman, FSST Sargeant at Arms Syed Huq, RST Member Robert “Bob” Walters, CRST Member Submitted via https://www.regulations.gov February 17, 2026 U.S Environmental Protection Agency 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW Washington D.C. 20460 RE: Docket ID. No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 Comment on proposed rule – Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations To the Environmental Protection Agency: I serve as Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Great Plains Tribal Water Alliance, Inc. The Tribal Water Alliance is chartered for the purposes of protecting the water rights of the Great Plains Tribes, reserved in our Treaties with the United States, and for advising the Great Plains Tribal Chairman’s Association on projects and policies affecting our water. The Board of Directors is comprised of representatives from the Standing Rock, Rosebud, Oglala, Lower Brule, Cheyenne River, Yankton and Flandreau Santee Sioux Tribes. I write on behalf of the Board, to express our strong opposition to the proposed rule diminishing the role of Tribes and other certifying authorities to protect our water under section 401 of the Clean Water Act. Our comments focus on three areas: (1) The proposed rule on water quality certification is part of a broader agenda to diminish protections for water; (2) EPA failed to engage in Nation-to-Nation Consultation; and (3) The proposed rule diminishes Tribal sovereignty and Transparency in Decision-making under the Clean Water Act. ____________________________________________________________________________________ P.O. Box 271 www.tribalwateralliance.org Pine Ridge, SD 57770 Letter to Environmental Protection Agency Docket ID. No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 February 17, 2026 Page Two The Proposed Rule is Part of a Broader Agenda to Diminish Protections for Water The Tribal Water Alliance is concerned with the proposed rule, taken in conjunction with other administrative actions by EPA. The proposed re-definition of “navigable waters,” also referred to as “waters of the United States,” will remove protections under the Clean Water Act to millions of acres of wetlands and important ephemeral waters. 90 Fed. Reg. 52498 (Nov. 20, 2025). The waters losing their protections under the revised definition produce valuable habitat for waterfowl and wildlife, and remove carbon from the atmosphere, at a time when greenhouse gas emissions are affecting our planet and our fresh water. On February 12, EPA announced a final rule rescinding the greenhouse gas emissions endangerment finding, which established the basis for the regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and motor vehicle standards under the Clean Air Act. https://www.epa.gov/regulations-emissions- vehicles-and-engines/final-rule-rescission-greenhouse-gas-endangerment. The proliferation of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere has caused persistent drought in the northern plains, enhancing the need to protect our valuable water. The proposed rule does the opposite. It would strip from Tribes and other certifying authorities our ability to influence decisions that affect the quality of our water. The multitude of proposed Clean Water and Clean Air Act rollbacks is staggering and poses severe implications for the Great Plains Tribes. EPA Failed to Engage in Nation-to-Nation Consultation For the Great Plains Tribes, Nation-to-Nation consultation is a Treaty right under Article 5 of the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868. 15 Stat. 635. This provision states in part: The United States agrees that the agent for said Indians shall… (conduct) prompt and diligent inquiry into such matters of complaint by and against the Indians as may be presented for investigation under the provisions of their Treaty stipulations. 15 Stat. 636. This Treaty right is exercised today pursuant to Executive Order 13175 on Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments. This executive order establishes the framework for the Nation-to-Nation relationship between the executive branch and the Indian Nations. Under E.O. 13175: ____________________________________________________________________________________ P.O. Box 271 www.tribalwateralliance.org Pine Ridge, SD 57770 Letter to Environmental Protection Agency Docket ID. No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 February 17, 2026 Page Three The United States continues to work with Indian tribes on government-to- government basis to address issues concerning tribal self government, tribal trust resources, and Indian tribal treaty and other rights…The United States recognizes the right of Indian tribes to self government and supports tribal sovereignty and self determination. Each agency shall have an accountable process to ensure meaningful and timely input by tribal officials in the development of regulatory policies that have tribal implications. 65 Fed. Reg. 67249-67250. Agencies such as EPA must promulgate their own policies to implement E.O. 13175. The EPA has issued its EPA Policy on Consultation with Indian Tribes (2023). According to the policy, “[C]onsultation meetings are government-to-government exchanges of information and dialogue between official representatives of the EPA and of federally-recognizes Tribal governments.” EPA Policy on Consultation with Indian Tribes, p. 5. The policy explicitly requires consultation prior to the issuance of “[r]egulations or rules.” Id. In the development of the proposed rule, EPA conducted no “prompt and diligent inquiry” into the concerns of the Great Plains Tribes on implementation of Clean Water Act section 401. 15 Stat. 636. There was no opportunity for “meaningful and timely input” by the Great Plains Tribes, as required in E.O. 13175. 65 Fed. Reg. 67249. Similarly, there were no “government-to- government exchanges of dialogue” in consultation meetings as required in the EPA Policy. https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-04/epa-policy-on-consultation-with-indian- tribes.pdf. Thus, EPA is violating article 5 of the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty, E.O. 13175 and the EPA Policy. A form letter, webinar and inter-Tribal staff level meetings do not constitute Nation-to- Nation consultation. 91 Fed. Reg. 2039. EPA’s failure to properly engage in the required Nation- to-Nation consultation with the Great Plains renders any final rule arbitrary and capricious within the meaning of the Administrative Procedures Act. 5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A). Moreover, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples requires the Tribes’ free, prior and informed consent to this diminishment of protections for Tribal waters. Consent has not been given. No final rule should be issued. ____________________________________________________________________________________ P.O. Box 271 www.tribalwateralliance.org Pine Ridge, SD 57770 Letter to Environmental Protection Agency Docket ID. No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 February 17, 2026 Page Four The Proposed Rule Diminishes Tribal Sovereignty and Transparency in Decision-making The proposed rule diminishes the Tribal role in implementing section 401 and undermines transparency in environmental decision-making. It eliminates the “additional contents” for applications currently required in 40 CFR §121.5(b)(5) & (6), thereby diminishing the available information for local decision-makers. The proposed rule also eliminates the requirement to analyze the “activity as a whole,” and requires Tribes to look at “discharge only.” That eliminates information needed for environmental decision-making, and violates Tribal sovereignty, the Clean Water Act itself and EPA’s mission to protect public health. In the preamble to the proposed rule, EPA endorses government-in-secrecy: [T]he proposed rule would limit any such materials to “water quality- related materials on any potential discharges.” Accordingly, applicants may redact or exclude… sensitive information…. The EPA acknowledges the desire of certifying authorities to have all necessary information as soon as possible in the certification process, but the Agency must balance that desire against the need for… certainty regarding the required contents of a request for certification. 91 Fed. Reg. 2019-2020. The proposed limits to the authority of Tribes (and other certifying authorities) to require information about a project’s environmental effects are highly problematic. The regulations should not limit the information to be made available to Tribes, or the authority of Tribes to certify projects based on their overall effect. Information should not be limited to “discharge only.” Sections 121.5(b) and (c) are important regulations for transparency and to enable Tribal leaders and the public to learn the overall environmental effects of proposed projects. EPA should not make any changes to these regulations. The only regulatory uncertainty was caused by EPA itself, when it issued the 2020 rule, upending regulations that had been in place for 50 years. The current proposed rule will cause uncertainty, by limiting the ability of Tribes and other certifying authorities to obtain information needed to determine the water quality impacts of proposed projects. It will also create confusion about timeframes for the approval or denial of certification, when applicants fail to provide sufficient information. That will result in needless litigation, which could further stress the Tribal role under section 401 of the Clean Water Act. ____________________________________________________________________________________ P.O. Box 271 www.tribalwateralliance.org Pine Ridge, SD 57770 Letter to Environmental Protection Agency Docket ID. No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 February 17, 2026 Page Five The proposed rule will diminish the opportunity for Tribes to certify whether federally- approved projects will impact the quality of Tribal waters. Indian water rights arise from our Treaties with the United States. The diminishment of protections for our water in the proposed rule violates the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe’s rights under the 1851 and 1868 Fort Laramie Treaties, as well as the Tribe’s role as prescribed in the Clean Water Act. There should be no changes to the TAS procedures in the absence of consultation and collaboration with Tribal leadership – which has not occurred. EPA has failed to explain in the preamble any rationale for the radical departure to the 2023 rule or to longstanding EPA policy in the implementation of Clean Water Act section 401 – in violation of the Administrative Procedures Act. Ultimately, the proposed rule violates Tribal sovereignty and our Treaty-guaranteed water rights, and is inconsistent with the Clean Water Act, which delineates a strong role for Tribes in decisions affecting Tribal waters. 33 U.S.C. §§1251(b), 1377. For these reasons, we oppose the proposed rule, and insist, in the strongest possible terms, that EPA abandon this rulemaking and get back to its mission of protecting public health and the environment, including our sacred water. Sincerely, Erroll “Doug” Crow Ghost, Jr., Chairman, Board of Directors Cc: Gay Kingman, Executive Director Great Plains Tribal Chairmen’s Association ____________________________________________________________________________________ P.O. Box 271 www.tribalwateralliance.org Pine Ridge, SD 57770

comment_text:
I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

comment_text:
*I strongly support increased transparency in property broker transactions as a necessary step toward fairness and accountability in the trucking industry. For too long, motor carriers and owner-operators have operated with limited visibility into brokered transactions, often resulting in disputes over payments and a lack of trust in the system.*

*By requiring brokers to disclose transaction records promptly and in an accessible format, FMCSA will create a more level playing field, ensuring that carriers receive fair compensation and can make informed business decisions. Transparency will deter unethical practices, improve industry stability, and promote fair competition.*

*I urge FMCSA to adopt strong enforcement measures to ensure compliance with these transparency rules. Without meaningful penalties for non-compliance, brokers may continue opaque practices that disadvantage carriers.*

*Thank you for considering this much-needed reform.*

*Sincerely,*

Gurtej Singh

comment_text: Comment to the Environmental Protection Agency Proposed Rule: Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations Benjamin Zycher* Senior Fellow, American Enterprise Institute February 17, 2026 RIN 2040-AG47 40 CFR Part 121, Document ID EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 FRL-6976.2-01-OW Federal Register Vol. 91, No. 10, Thursday January 15, 2026, pp. 2008-2042 Submitted through the federalregister.gov portal at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/15/2026-00754/updating- the-water-quality-certification-regulations#open-comment This comment paper addresses the regulatory policy issues attendant upon the EPA proposal to revise the 2023 rule establishing processes for implementation of Section 401 of the Clean Water Act.1 At the most general level, the proposed rule represents a vast improvement over the 2023 final rule, in particular because the 2023 final rule facilitates massive obstruction of important infrastructure projects with little or no protection of water quality as defined in the CWA. Indeed, such obstructionism based upon section 401 often has been justified on grounds unrelated to water quality. At the same time, some improvements to the proposed rule are advisable. This comment is organized as follows. Summary. I. Examples of Projects Blocked or Delayed Using Improper Applications of Section 401. II. Reforms In the Proposed Rule That Should Be Finalized. III. Ways to Strengthen the Proposed Rule. IV. Conclusions. * Ph.D., Economics, University of California, Los Angeles. Senior fellow, American Enterprise Institute. The views expressed are solely those of the author. I can be reached at benjamin.zycher@aei.org. 1 The 2026 proposed rule is at https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-01-15/pdf/2026-00754.pdf. For the 2023 EPA final rule, see Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule, 88 FR 66558 (September 27, 2023). The American Enterprise Institute (AEI) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit, 501(c)(3) educational organization and does not take institutional positions on any issues. The views expressed in this testimony are those of the author. 2 Summary Section 401 of the Clean Water Act, as implemented in the 2023 final rule, allows for lengthy obstructionism of important infrastructure projects on grounds that are perverse economically and environmentally. Several examples are discussed below. The proposed rule contains several provisions that should be finalized: • Limiting the Scope of the CWA Section 401 to Actual Discharges. • Reforming Timeline Withdrawal and Resubmission Delays. • Standardizing Request Parameters. • Requiring Joint Agreement to Certification Modifications. • Establishing A Firm Hearing and Determinization Timeline for Neighboring-State Objections. Two areas of recommended strengthening are as follows: • Strengthen the Withdrawal/Resubmission Prohibition. • Specifying Categories for Neighboring State “May Affect” Determinations. I. Examples of Projects Blocked or Delayed Using Improper Applications of Section 401 It is no secret that obstruction of new energy infrastructure projects is a massive undertaking by ideological opponents of conventional (fossil, hydropower, and other) energy, by not-in-my-backyard interests, and by rent-seeking opponents of projects that would strengthen competitive conditions in specific markets.2 Section 401 of the CWA has been used repeatedly for that purpose, with arguments having little or nothing to do with water quality. A few examples are as follows. • The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation in 2016 denied approval for the Constitution Pipeline, which would have transported natural gas from the Marcellus basin in Pennsylvania to markets in New York via the Iroquois Gas Transmission and to New England via the Tennessee Gas Pipeline. NYSDEC cited climate change concerns and downstream greenhouse gas emissions from utilization of the natural gas supplies. With respect to water quality — after all, the central focus of the CWA — NYSDEC denied the application for a water quality certification on the grounds that Constitution had failed to provide information on stream crossings, and made reference to the purported "resistance" by Constitution in terms of responding adequately to NYSDEC's requests. Nowhere was there any determination in the denial of adverse effects on water quality.3 • NYSDEC in 2017 denied approval for the Millennium Valley Lateral pipeline, on 2 On reform of the implementing regulations for the National Environmental Policy Act, see Benjamin Zycher at https://www.aei.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Zycher_CEQ_NEPA_Comment_Nov_2021.pdf. 3 See https://uk.practicallaw.thomsonreuters.com/w-012- 8378?transitionType=Default&contextData=(sc.Default)&firstPage=true. New York now has opposed Constitution’s proposal to FERC to reissue its permit for the pipeline. See https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/ny-regulators-oppose-filings-proposed-constitution-pipeline-project-2026- 01-28/., 3 endangered species grounds and a purported inadequate FERC review with respect to greenhouse gas emissions.4 Those rationales have little to do with water quality. FERC later that year overturned the NYSDEC denial, on the grounds that NYSDEC had waived its certification authority by failing to act within the one-year statutory deadline, and was upheld by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.5 • The Washington State Department of Ecology in 2017 denied a water quality permit sought by Millennium Bulk Terminals to construct and operate a coal export terminal in Longview, WA, on the grounds that the terminal would have caused “significant and unavoidable harm” to nine environmental areas: air quality, vehicle traffic, vessel traffic, rail capacity, rail safety, [train] noise pollution, social and community resources, cultural resources, and tribal resources. The project parameters related to water quality were trivial: 24 acres of wetlands, 41.5 acres of dredging in the Columbia riverbed, and 537 pilings in the Columbia river. • The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection in 2019 denied the PennEast Pipeline permit application incomplete, in a real-life “Catch-22” scenario in which the state denied PennEast’s eminent domain application for state-owned land, thus denying PennEast access to land for which the state required surveys.6 Despite winning at the Supreme Court on the eminent domain issue, PennEast cancelled the project in 2021, citing permitting difficulties.7 II. Reforms In the Proposed Rule That Should Be Finalized Limiting the Scope of the CWA Section 401 to Actual Discharges. The 2023 final rule implemented an “activity as a whole” definition for regulatory oversight of the certification process. This is inconsistent with the law, and the proposed rule returns the focus of certification requirements to actual point source discharges into the waters of the United States. Section 401(a)(1) requires certification for projects “which may result in any discharge into the navigable waters.” Certification must ensure “that any such discharge will comply with the applicable provisions of” the enumerated CWA sections.8 This shift from “activity as a whole” to “discharge” is consistent with the 1972 statutory change from “activity” to “discharge.” Reforming Timeline Withdrawal and Resubmission Delays. Ideological and special interests and agencies intent upon obstructing given projects often have circumvented the statutory 4 See Weiler and Stanford at https://www.eba-net.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/21-503-540-Weiler_FINAL.pdf. 5 See, respectively, https://anzlaw.thomsonreuters.com/w-010- 3851?originationContext=document&transitionType=DocumentItem&contextData=(sc.Default)&ppcid=15a87f064 3334f16b6bc87f02cde528f&firstPage=true and https://www.troutmanenergyreport.com/2018/03/second-circuit- affirms-ferc-ruling-ny-dec-waived-authority-cwa-permit-pipeline-project/. 6 See https://aglaw.psu.edu/shale-law-in-the-spotlight/penn-east-pipeline-project-u-s-court-of-appeals-denies- eminent-domain-proceedings-by-penneast-pipeline-company-llc-for-the-acquisition-of-new-jersey-state-owned- properties/. 7 See https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/20pdf/19-1039_8n5a.pdf and paragraph 9 at https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/C-2- 022020.pdf#:~:text=24%20The%20record%20demonstrates%20that,to%20commence%20and%20complete%20con struction. 8 See 33 U.S.C. § 1341(a)(1). 4 one-year deadline by advising applicants to withdraw and resubmit proposals, thus restarting the one-year clock, sometimes repeatedly. The proposed rule prohibits certifying authorities from circumventing the deadline through the withdrawal-and-resubmission process. It adds that “the certifying authority may not request the applicant to withdraw a request for certification or take any action to extend the reasonable period of time” beyond the explicit “shall not exceed one year” language of Section 401(a)(1).9 The obvious Congressional intent was to prevent agencies under Section 401 from ending project proposals by delaying them indefinitely. Standardizing Request Parameters. The proposed rule proscribes agencies from adding required parameters for certification applications, thus returning the process to a single federal standard for a complete application. This provision would be consistent with the Second Circuit decision in NYSDEC that the “plain language of Section 401 outlines a bright-line rule regarding the beginning of review.”10 Allowing agencies to decide when applications are “complete” would enable them to delay even the consideration of project proposals indefinitely. Requiring Joint Agreement to Certification Modifications. The proposed rule requires that the relevant federal agency, the certifying agency, and the applicant agree to modifications of certifications already issued before any modifications are implemented, and the applicant must agree to the language of the modification. This provision of the proposed rule avoids an obvious bait-and-switch problem affecting not only given projects but the project investment process writ large. It also avoids the problem of agencies using the modification process to extent the review deadlines beyond the one-year statutory limit. Establishing A Firm Hearing and Determinization Timeline for Neighboring-State Objections. Section 401(a)(2) establishes specific timeframes for each part of the neighboring- state objection process, except for the public hearing component. States notified that a certification may affect their water quality requirements have sixty days to determine whether a discharge “will violate” those requirements, but the CWA does not specify the timing limits on the public hearing process and the final ruling by the federal agency. The proposed rule establishes a 90-day time limit for the public hearing and final determination process. This is necessary to avoid unreasonable delays. III. Ways to Strengthen the Proposed Rule Strengthen Withdrawal/Resubmission Prohibition. EPA asks for comments on whether the proposed text “sufficiently addresses the regulatory uncertainty surrounding withdrawal and resubmission.” Additional specificity would be useful. The final rule should make it clear that the one-year timeline begins with the initial receipt of a complete application, regardless of any subsequent withdrawal initiated or requested by the agency. Specifying Categories for Neighboring State “May Affect” Determinations. EPA asks for comments on categories for “may affect” determinations with respect to other states’ water quality. Exclusions should include discharges into waters with no hydrologic connection to other states, small and/or temporary discharges that cannot flow to other states, and discharges in isolated coastal areas with no bodies of water shared with other states. 9 Ibid. 10 See 884 F.3d at 455–56. 5 IV. Conclusions This proposed rule imposes important limits on CWA Section 401 agency obstruction of important infrastructure projects, driven by opposition ideological, political, and economic. These limits should be finalized. There are a few areas in which the proposed rule could be strengthened, which the final rule should reflect.

comment_text:
I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

It offers actionable requests, but the argument would be stronger with citations, data, or more specific evidence supporting the allergenicity and contamination concerns.

Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, I'm a retired U.S. EPS career employee who witnessed first hand serious water quality issues that harmed people's health and their recreational opportunities and caused significant financial burden to local governments and other entities. I've written about water quality and quantity issues quite often and can say with 100% certainty that water quality and quantity are inseparable. If you degrade water quality enough, that water actually becomes polluted water, as is obvious, and polluted water is more closely related to cesspool contamination than it is to what we have almost always understood to be water. Polluted water, as just one example, "killed" Lake Erie and Lake Erie's commercial fishing and recreational boating and angling industries. While Lake Erie has recovered some of its former commercial fishing and boating and angling industries, still extremely expensive water quality issues have harmed drinking water quality, rendering Lake Erie's water unsuitable for drinking water use in Toledo, Ohio, as one recent example. The new water quality issues under today's regulatory requirements differ from those of the past because these are new, such as the advent of "harmful algae blooms," invasive species and other threats superimposed upon just about all previous threats. So, rather than allow myself to go on about the issues of degraded waters, I conducted a quick AI search, which is provided below and covers the most current major issues, yet does not capture the true gravity of what is at stake for Americans and the reputation and dignity of America itself. "What is the danger of releasing clean water protections federally? "AI Overview Redefining "Waters of the United States" (WOTUS) to exclude wetlands and small streams—a move often spurred by Supreme Court rulings like Sackett v. EPA—removes federal protection for millions of acres of aquatic ecosystems. This deregulation risks significant increases in water pollution, heightened flood risks, destruction of wildlife habitats, and decreased drinking water quality. Key Dangers of Reclassifying Wetlands and Small Streams: Increased Flood Risks and Reduced Natural Protection: Wetlands act as natural sponges, absorbing floodwaters and storm surges. Removing protection allows for development in these areas, making surrounding communities more vulnerable to flooding. Widespread Water Pollution: Small, ephemeral streams and wetlands filter pollutants before they reach larger rivers and lakes. Without federal oversight, these areas can be filled, paved over, or used for waste disposal, increasing pollution in connected, larger water bodies. Loss of Biodiversity: Wetlands provide crucial habitats for wildlife, including endangered species. The removal of protections can accelerate the destruction of these habitats and threaten the survival of various fish and species. Reduced Drinking Water Protection: Many municipalities rely on small streams and headwaters that feed into larger water sources. Removing safeguards for these smaller, upstream waters directly impacts the quality of downstream drinking water sources. Regulatory Inconsistency and Increased Burden on States: While intended to reduce federal overreach on private landowners, this change shifts the responsibility to states, many of which may lack the resources or regulatory frameworks to protect these water bodies effectively." Thank you for all of the incredibly important work that you do at the U.S. EPA. All of the best to you and your agency. Thomas J. Slabe Sincerely, Thomas Dewittville, NY

comment_text:
Benefits of using brokers

Large shippers look for brokers for efficient access to the transportation marketplace and the broker pool is an amalgamated capacity in the eyes of the shipper. The shippers and carriers need brokers who have invested in technology and people power such that they can amalgamate carrier capacity that is not otherwise available to shippers. Those  investments cost money and if a broker is charging too much, the broker will be priced out because the carrier can go directly to large carriers, etc. In many cases, carriers experience a cost savings and increased revenue as a result of brokers arranging the freight. Savings that the carriers can experience include through administrative functions and other e0iciencies brokers provide to the owner/operator. Shippers and carriers both benefit from transfer of transportation risk to the broker in large part. This extra layer of broker protection also comes with a market and operational expertise that cannot be replicated by either the shipper or the carrier. The largest businesses in America utilize brokers to arrange their transportation as do smaller businesses for these reasons. 

True costs and value from utilizing brokers

The rule as proposed aims to provide transparency, however the method the FMCSA uses to approach rate transparency is not an accurate representation of anything meaningful. The rule as proposed would require the broker to disclose the rate the shipper pays the broker to arrange the transportation and the rate at which the broker hires the carrier. The incorrect approach is to view the di0erence in these rates as a profit. It is not. Brokers continually invest in technology to combat fraud as well as inefficiencies in the marketplace. Brokers invest in communication systems that make doing business more effective on both the shipper and carrier ends. Fraud and theft prevention is the greatest challenge to the U.S. transportation system today. Broker investment in and focus on fraud and theft prevention is something neither the shipper nor the carriers have time to solve. It is the body of good broker citizens who are leading the way toward solving the biggest epidemic to plague the highways. We encourage the FMCSA to focus its efforts in this area and discover you have a willing marketplace partner to support innovation in greater freight security. Brokers invest in staff who handle critical processes in the supply chain. Brokers invest in insurance coverages that potentially add a layer of assurance and security to both the shipper and carrier, depending on the circumstance. All of those costs, and others, remain unseen in the way the FMCSA approaches rate transparency. To force this disclosure requirement on brokers is unconscionable because it is not a fair representation of the value added to the supply chain brokers provide nor does truthfully represent the business costs that come with operating a business that provides these benefits to the market.

rationales.relevance: The comment is clearly about broker transparency and the value of brokers, which is directly related to FMCSA broker rate disclosure issues. However, it does not engage the docket in a detailed or specific way beyond general opposition to the proposed rule.
rationales.reasoning: The argument is generally understandable and internally consistent: brokers provide value, incur costs, and rate differences should not be treated as pure profit. Still, the reasoning is mostly asserted rather than developed, and some claims are broad or repetitive.
rationales.evidence: The comment provides no citations, data, studies, or concrete examples. It relies entirely on general assertions about brokers, fraud prevention, and market benefits without supporting evidence.
rationales.impact: It claims the rule would misrepresent broker value and unfairly burden brokers, but the likely real-world impacts are described in broad terms only. The comment does not quantify harms or explain specific operational consequences in detail.
rationales.actionability: The only clear request is that FMCSA focus on fraud and theft prevention instead of rate transparency. This is a directionally useful suggestion, but it is not a detailed or feasible regulatory alternative.
rationales.structure_formatting: The comment is divided into two thematic sections, which helps readability, but it is still a dense block of text with repetition and some grammatical issues. The formatting is basic and not especially polished.
rationales.overall: This is a relevant but largely unsupported advocacy comment. It communicates a clear position in favor of brokers and against the proposed transparency approach, but it lacks evidence, specificity, and concrete regulatory recommendations.

overall_summary: The comment is on-topic and clearly opposes the proposed broker transparency approach, but it is mostly a general policy argument rather than a well-supported submission. Its main weaknesses are the absence of evidence, limited specificity about impacts, and only modestly actionable recommendations.

comment_text: From: hansen1167@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 2/9/2026 4:32:42 PM Subject: Docket ID# EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 — Opposition to Proposed 2026 Changes to Circumscribe Certification Authority of States and Tribes -------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from hansen1167@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, I am writing this afternoon in strong opposition to the Environment Protections Agency's proposed 2026 rule changes which seek to circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water. The EPA is the very entity that reported that water resource stewardship done by Tribal Nations has a higher bar and exceeds the EPAs standards. (Ending the Interminable Gap in Indian Country Water Quality Protection,” Harvard Environmental Law Review, Vol. 45, No. 1, 2020-21| Author: James Grijalva.) We should not take away Tribal water sovereignty or right to be treated as a state. We all benefit from the economic benefits of Tribal stewarded and rehabilitated land, and the public and private money that follows these projects as local investments. It also helps to eliminate the high cost of pollution mitigation and reduce disruption to household water supplies, whether city water or a well. We should be transferring more land to Tribal Nations to be stewarded, not less. The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. The proposed rule change goes against the common good. The EPA’s proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. The 2026 certification rules proposed by the EPA are unlawful and unreasonable. My opposition is specifically regarding... 1. ) The Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations. 2. ) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. 3. ) I am opposed to all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water. 4. ) I'm opposed to the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 5. ) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? Please, I urge you, the EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a better job of protecting all of us from contaminated water, whether for drinking, swimming, or fishing. Thank you for your work and for consideration of my comments. Sincerely, Jaden Hansen 2141 Minneapolis Ave Minneapolis, MN 55406-4239 hansen1167@gmail.com

rationales.relevance: The comment directly addresses the proposed EPA rule on state and Tribal certification authority and responds to multiple specific changes listed in the docket.
rationales.reasoning: The letter presents a coherent opposition argument, linking the rule changes to clean water protection, Tribal sovereignty, and state authority. Some claims are more rhetorical than analytically developed, but the overall logic is clear.
rationales.evidence: It includes a citation to a Harvard Environmental Law Review article and references Minnesota water bodies and general Clean Water Act purposes, but it lacks detailed data, legal citations, or concrete supporting evidence for many assertions.
rationales.impact: The commenter identifies plausible harms such as reduced Tribal sovereignty, weaker pollution controls, and risks to drinking water and aquatic resources, though the impacts are stated broadly rather than quantified.
rationales.actionability: The comment clearly asks EPA to reject or withdraw the proposed rule and objects to several specific provisions, making the requested action understandable and feasible.
rationales.structure_formatting: The letter is readable and organized around numbered objections, but it is somewhat informal, repetitive, and includes emotionally charged language that reduces polish.
rationales.overall: This is a strong public comment because it is highly relevant and clearly opposes the rule with specific objections. It would be stronger with more detailed evidence and a more formal, concise presentation.

overall_summary: A relevant and forceful comment that clearly opposes the proposed rule and identifies several specific concerns. Its main weaknesses are limited evidentiary support and a somewhat informal, rhetorical style, but it remains a solid public comment overall.

I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

It is somewhat less focused on specific docket questions because those are not provided.

overall_summary: A solid, clearly written comment that directly challenges labeling and safety issues for a synthetic-biology-derived color additive. It is persuasive in tone and specific in requests, but it would be stronger with citations, data, or regulatory support for its claims.

comment_text:
I am commenting on Docket ID # EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 and want to share my strong objections to the proposed rule change.
These changes would circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water.

The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. 

The EPA’s proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. The EPA’s proposed 2026 certification rules are unlawful, unreasonable, and just plain wrong. Specifically:

1.) I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations.

2.) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park.

3.) I oppose all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water.

4.) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 

5.) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? 

The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish.

Thank you for considering my comments,

comment_text: 2/17/2026 RE: 91 FR 2008 To those responsible for considering: We are the Environmental Law Society (ELS) of Vermont Law and Graduate School. We are a student organization whose purpose is to promote environmental awareness and provide a forum for student participation in projects and action concerning current environmental issues. ELS strives to affect global, national, statewide, and local issues by pursuing specific goals and cooperating with other environmental groups. ELS provides a forum for critique and support of the legal system, current laws and regulations, and actions undertaken by other groups which concern the environment. We are first-, second-, and third-year law students, LLM students, and Masters’ students who are deeply concerned about the Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed “clarifications” and procedural updates to the Clean Water Act Section 401 certification process. I. Background The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is charged with protecting “human health and the environment.”1 The EPA is the Administrator of the Clean Water Act (CWA) and oversees the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES). 33 U.S.C. § 1251(d); 33 U.S.C. § 1342. A permit issued by the EPA pursuant to NPDES is different from, but relevant to, the State permit program. 33 U.S.C. § 1342(b). The permitting program discerns between permissible, anticipated, or informed introductions of “pollutants,” and those that are impermissible. Foremost, the overarching purpose of the CWA and accompanying permitting system is “to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a). Section 401 of the CWA is unique; it grants authority to states and tribes (those identified as receiving “treatment in a similar manner as a State” (TAS)) to permit or deny proposed activities that result in a discharge into waters of the United States and require a CWA permit. Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 2008 (Jan. 15, 2026). The EPA may act as a certifying authority where there is no authorized state or tribe, but otherwise, Congress granted the states and tribes authorization over certification directly. 33 U.S.C. § 1341(a)(1). Under Section 401, a CWA permit may not be granted without 401 certification unless certification by a state or tribe is waived. Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 2010 (Jan. 15, 2026). Certification indicates the proposed permit meets state or tribal 1 https://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/our-mission-and-what-we-do water quality standards and effluent guidelines, as well as other appropriate provisions of state or tribal law.2 401 certification thus enables a “robust State and Tribal role in [] Federal licensing and permitting . . .” Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 2010 (Jan. 15, 2026). II. Proposed 2026 Changes Certification provisions were changed for the first time in 50 years during the first Trump Administration pursuant to an Executive Order (Promoting Energy Infrastructure and Economic Growth) in direct conflict with established law. Clean Water Act Section 401 Certification Rule, 85 Fed. Reg. 42210 (July 13, 2020); See generally PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County v. Was. Dep’t of Ecology, 511 U.S. 700 (1994). The 2020 rule limited the review of states and tribes generally from addressing a permitted activity “as a whole” in their certification review. Id. at 712. This was a stark contrast to over 50 years of operating as enacted. Exemplifying state dissatisfaction with the change, the 2020 rule was vacated by the U.S. District Court for Northern District of California. See In re Clean Water Act Rulemaking, 568 F. Supp. 3d 1013 (Ca. N.D., 2021). The 2020 rule was stayed by a U.S. Supreme Court emergency docket decision. Louisiana v. American Rivers, 569 U.S. 1 (2022). The last final rule on the matter, promulgated in 2023, reinstated the “activity as a whole” provision which enables state and tribe authority over the same certification decisions since the CWA’s enactment. Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule, 88 Fed. Reg. 66558 (September 27, 2023). The complicated history of section 401is befuddled with the EPA’s recent decision to revise the rule again. In the 2026 certification rule, the review of states and tribes will again be choked to the limiting standards seen in 2020. Essentially, this means “certifying authorities cannot consider water quality impacts to waters beyond the waters of the United States receiving the discharge(s) from [a] project.”3 In July 2025, the EPA requested input on regulatory uncertainty and implementation changes under the 2023 rule. States, tribes, industry members, and the public were invited to provide their input. The Summary Report for the tribal consultation was profound: almost unanimous interest to keep the 2023 rule.4 Specifically, the report noted, “[s]everal Tribes noted the activity-based scope of certification and the other related definitions (e.g., water quality requirements, applicable waters, etc.) provide 2 https://www.nawm.org/wetlands-law/cwa/clean-water-act-section-401-water-quality-certification.html 3 https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-01/cwa401_proposed-rule-economic- analysis_jan2026_508c.pdf at page 15 4 https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-01/cwa401_tribal-consultation-summary- jan2026_508c.pdf. The report adds: “In their input, the Tribes unanimously support the definitions and procedures promulgated under the 2023 Rule, asserting the 2023 Rule had successfully facilitated Tribal water quality protections without creating implementation challenges or regulatory uncertainty. The Tribes urged the EPA to retain the current regulations and uphold its trust responsibility to Tribal nations.” Id. Tribes the authority to holistically evaluate the range of possible impacts a federally licensed or permitted project may have on water quality.” Id. The Summary Report from the states’ consultation was identical: “State agencies and State associations expressed concern and cautioned against revising the scope of certification and associated definitions. A few State agencies and State associations asserted the EPA lacks evidence to support their claims of implementation challenges with the 2023 Rule, and expressed concern the EPA may return to inflexible, administratively burdensome processes that created implementation challenges.”5 Both states and tribes, entities authorized by Congress to certify CWA permits in their jurisdiction, relayed that the operational process under the 2023 rule is unproblematic, procedurally efficient, and balances sovereign interests well. Another significant change in the proposed 2026 rule includes limiting the conditions states and tribes may impose on a certification. Specifically, it narrows review to water quality concerns as opposed to the accepted general environmental protection concerns. The economic analysis announced alongside the proposed rule concluded that the number of conditional permit certifications decreases. The reduction arises because of increasing project developments, but the blatant fallacy is assuming that states and tribes will be more likely to certify projects when the Administrator has tightened its fist. In reality, reducing review will create a less trustworthy and transparent process by incentivizing sovereign entities to bolster their water quality standards and outright deny permits rather than suggest conditional permits. This presents an unfortunate outcome if the goal is to expedite development. III. The EPA is exceeding its statutory authority The EPA has exceeded its statutory authority under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) by proposing a rule unsupported by substantial evidence. Agency actions are reviewed by courts under the APA, which “delineates the basic contours of judicial review.” Loper Bright Enters v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 391 (2024). The court reviews and sets aside agency actions that are found arbitrary or capricious; a denial of a statutory right; contrary to constitutional right; in excess of jurisdiction or authority; based on erroneous facts; unwarranted by substantial evidence; or otherwise contrary to law. 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A-F). Additionally, the Chevron doctrine guided statutory interpretation when reviewing statues administered by agencies. Loper Bright Enters v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 379 (2024). The Chevron doctrine required heavy deference to agency action by the reviewing court. Loper Bright Enters v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 379 (2024). Loper Bright, however, overruled Chevron and now requires courts to 5 https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2026-01/cwa401_federalism-consultation- summary_jan2026_508c.pdf exercise their “independent judgement” when deciding whether agency action adhered to its statutory authority. Loper Bright Enters v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 412 (2024). The EPA has exceeded its statutory authority under the APA by making decisions unsupported by substantial evidence. The agency sought tribal and state input which yielded disinterest for less involvement in the CWA permitting process. Local communities know best how to manage their ecosystems, and the EPA is interfering with local efforts. Conditional permit issuance is a necessary compromise when competing interests. The EPA is also failing to uphold its statutory responsibility to protect “human health and the environment.” https://www.epa.gov/aboutepa/our- mission-and-what-we-do. The primary focus of the EPA should not be overlooked when the current system is unproblematic and functioning. Any reviewing court should not defer to the EPA when deciding the legality of the proposed rule that is unsupported by substantial evidence and unpopular by the groups most affected by the change in procedure. With deep concern, VLGS Environmental Law Society | ELS@vermontlaw.edu

comment_text: From: singingalltheway@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 2/15/2026 12:20:50 PM Subject: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 ----------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from singingalltheway@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, The Great Lakes, the greatest system of surface freshwater in the world, rely on wetlands, rivers, and streams to filter pollution, prevent flooding in our communities, and support fishing and recreation. It is critical that the U.S. EPA sticks to its mission to enforce environmental laws and defend, not degrade, the Clean Water Act. The proposed rule change to Section 401 seeks to take control away from states and Tribes, thus loosening the clean water protections strongly supported by most Americans regardless of political affiliation. In particular: - Changing this part of the Clean Water Act betrays the idea of federal and state cooperation, which is foundational to America's system of government. - This limits states' and Tribes' opportunities to prioritize their specific needs to protect their water. - Weakening Section 401 undermines the will of Americans who want clean water protections. - Shortening project reviews does not allow states and Tribes adequate time to thoroughly assess projects that may increase pollution. I am especially concerned that further weakening of clean water protections will harm waters in the Great Lakes, a vital resource that tens of millions of residents depend upon for drinking water and our economy. Such a change will likely have a cascading effect, eventually harming sources of freshwater around the country. This proposed rule change will further strip protections of wetlands, which provide significant regional economic benefits, such as: - Supporting recreational activities that bring in $50 billion annually to the region - Filtering out pollution to keep Great Lakes water clean for drinking and recreation - Controlling flooding, reducing damage and costs to communities and homes For the reasons of popular national support, regional economic implications, the official mission of the U.S. EPA, and in support of states and Tribal rights, I urge you to fully enforce the Clean Water Act and maintain the authority of states and Tribes to protect clean water. Sincerely, Marianne Watertown, MA

comment_text: STATE OF LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL P.O. BOX 94005 BATON ROUGE, LA 70804-9005 February 17, 2026 The Honorable Lee Zeldin Administrator U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 1200 Pennsylvania Ave., NW Washington, DC 20460 Re: Comments of Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Wyoming on EPA’s Proposed Rule “Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations” Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 Dear Administrator Zeldin: The States of Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Wyoming appreciate the opportunity to comment on EPA’s proposed revisions to the regulations implementing Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. 91 Fed. Reg. 2,008 (Jan. 15, 2026). The States support EPA’s goals of improving regulatory clarity, administrative efficiency, and timely decision-making. Clear, administrable rules benefit States, federal permitting agencies, and regulated entities alike. Section 401 reflects the Clean Water Act’s cooperative federalism framework. Congress tied certification to “discharges” while preserving the States’ primary authority to apply and enforce water quality standards within their borders. Maintaining this balance—clear federal limits paired with meaningful State implementation—honors congressional intent, protects State sovereignty, and promotes consistent water quality protection. A final rule must remain faithful to the statutory text Congress enacted, neither expanding nor contracting the role Section 401 assigns to the States. Given the repeated changes to Section 401 regulations in recent years, regulatory stability is critical. The final rule should provide a durable framework that can be consistently implemented across administrations. I. Scope of Certification Review The States agree that Section 401 is a discharge-focused provision. The statute directs certifying authorities to determine whether “any such discharge” will comply 1 STATE OF LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL P.O. BOX 94005 BATON ROUGE, LA 70804-9005 with applicable provisions of the CWA and water quality requirements. A discharge- focused scope provides necessary limiting principles, promotes national consistency, and reduces litigation risk by ensuring certification is not used to regulate matters untethered to the water quality impacts of a discharge. Clear and nationally consistent guardrails also reduce the risk of forum shopping and uneven application among States, promoting greater stability for all stakeholders. At the same time, a discharge-focused scope does not eliminate State judgment. Within Congress’s statutory boundaries, States must retain authority to apply their water quality standards—including designated uses, narrative and numeric criteria, and antidegradation requirements—to determine compliance. The scope limitation defines what is being certified, not who makes the determination. This includes the ability to apply duly adopted water quality standards and implementing regulations approved or recognized under the Act, consistent with statutory limits. EPA should clarify that certifying authorities may evaluate discharge characteristics and reasonably foreseeable impacts necessary to determine compliance, while excluding indirect, speculative, or attenuated effects lacking a clear causal nexus to the discharge. States must also retain authority to impose conditions clearly linked to assuring discharge compliance. A discharge-focused, nexus-based framework best reflects the statutory text and supports durable, consistent implementation. II. Certification of General Permits and Federal Projects The States urge EPA to retain a clear and workable approach to certification of general permits and federally authorized projects where discharges are subject to Section 401. States have historically applied water quality standards in these contexts, ensuring discharge compliance at the appropriate stage. Unduly narrowing certification risks creating regulatory gaps and shifting discharge compliance issues to later permitting stages, resulting in duplicative review, inconsistent requirements, and uncertainty. Clear delineation of when certification applies promotes national consistency and reduces litigation over the scope of Section 401. The States seek clarity to ensure water quality considerations remain predictably integrated into federal decision-making. III. Certification Application Completeness and Statutory Review Period The States agree that the one-year statutory deadline is mandatory and that clarity regarding when the review period begins is important. However, meaningful review 2 STATE OF LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL P.O. BOX 94005 BATON ROUGE, LA 70804-9005 depends on sufficient information to evaluate compliance with applicable water quality requirements. States rely on State statutes and regulations to determine completeness. These requirements are designed to ensure that certifying authorities have the information necessary to conduct a technically sound review. An inflexible federal standard could trigger the review period before adequate information is available, undermining defensibility and increasing the risk of disputes and litigation. EPA should establish minimum federal elements while preserving State authority to require additional water-quality-relevant information before the review period begins. This approach balances predictability with sound decision-making. At the same time, the States support procedural clarity that ensures certification decisions are timely, well- documented, and grounded in identified water quality requirements. IV. Certification Conditions The States agree that certification conditions must be tied to compliance with applicable water quality requirements and should not be used to regulate matters unrelated to water quality. Section 401 should function as a water quality compliance tool, not as a generalized land-use or permitting authority beyond the discharge compliance determination Congress prescribed. At the same time, limiting conditions to monitoring alone would unduly constrain the States’ ability to assure compliance. Monitoring is not always sufficient to prevent violations. States must retain authority to impose substantive, preventative conditions clearly linked to discharge compliance. EPA should clarify the required nexus while preserving State discretion within those bounds. V. Modification of Certifications The States recognize the importance of predictability and reliance interests for regulated entities. Frequent regulatory shifts and constrained implementation tools can undermine confidence in the Section 401 process and require States and applicants alike to repeatedly adjust to new requirements. States also face increased administrative and legal burdens when they lack adequate tools to address new information or evolving compliance concerns over the life of a permitted discharge. Certification modification authority has long been an essential tool to address new information, changed circumstances, or noncompliance affecting water quality. Requiring applicant consent as a prerequisite to certification modification would unduly restrict State authority to ensure ongoing compliance with 3 STATE OF LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE OFFICE OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL P.O.
