comment_text: Monday, February 16, 2026 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency EPA Docket Center Water Docket Mail Code 28221T 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW Washington, DC 20460 Subject: Retain or Strengthen State & Tribal Clean Water Act Authority -- Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations (Document ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929-0001) To EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin: I strongly oppose the Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act Section 401 water quality certification regulations. The proposed rule’s regulatory changes would reduce the ability of states and tribes to evaluate the overall impacts of a federal infrastructure project on local waterways. Implementing this rule will upend decades of precedent, strip key powers from states and tribes, and dramatically undermine protections for clean water in the United States, putting drinking water sources, rivers, wetlands, and downstream communities at risk while making it easier for polluting projects to move forward without accountability. We don’t need to “streamline” fossil fuel infrastructure or new dams, especially at the expense of our waterways. “It is horrifying that we have to fight our own government to save the environment.” -- Ansel Adams This proposal comes immediately after Environmental Protection Agency’s rollback of federal water protections under the Waters of the United States. Together, these actions undermine the Clean Water Act’s purpose and threaten water quality, public health, and local economies. The Clean Water Act empowers states and tribes to examine how federal infrastructure projects, including pipelines, may impact local water quality. For 50 years, Section 401 of the Clean Water Act has provided essential protection for our nation’s waterways by giving states and tribes the important opportunity to weigh in on federally permitted projects and ensure the continued health of their waterways, environment, and people. When a state or tribe determines that an infrastructure project harms local waterways, they can leverage Section 401 of the Clean Water Act to reject infrastructure permits. This structure of cooperative federalism was central to the original design of the Clean Water Act. Every state is unique when it comes to the types of waterways it has, the ways in which those waterways support people and the economy and the challenges it faces in ensuring the continued health of those waterways. Because of this, states are in a better position than the federal government to understand the impacts of a proposed project and to come up with a plan to mitigate those impacts. “As we peer into society’s future, we—you and I, and our government—must avoid the impulse to live only for today, plundering for our own ease and convenience the Page 1 of 4 precious resources of tomorrow. We cannot mortgage the material assets of our grandchildren without risking the loss also of their political and spiritual heritage. We want democracy to survive for all generations to come, not to become the insolvent phantom of tomorrow.” -- Dwight D. Eisenhower The proposed rule would significantly limit Section 401 authority by restricting reviews to only “direct discharges” into waterways, rather than allowing comprehensive assessments of broader environmental impacts. The reduced scope of Section 401 under the proposed rule could result in damage to waterways other than through direct pollution. This change would weaken local communities’ ability to protect drinking water sources, fisheries, wetlands, and cultural resources, thereby cutingt off drinking water, disrupting the migration of aquatic animals, and destroying natural floodplains. The proposed rule would also narrow the scope of tribal oversight by requiring that they evaluate projects through a separate authorization program. If finalized, this proposed rule would impose greater demands on tribes to prove that they have large-scale capacity to undergo a rigorous review of federal projects, even as much of the country grapples with restricted local government funding. Reducing the scope of the Clean Water Act’s Section 401 to only account for how direct discharges into waterways impact water quality will hinder the ability of state and tribal governments to fully consider how projects impact local communities and wildlife, with possible threats to public health, natural environments, and local economies. The proposed revisions would unlawfully and dangerously narrow the authority of states and tribes to protect their waters from harmful projects—especially large oil and gas pipelines. Furthermore, the proposed strict deadlines and limited review scope would accelerate project approvals without ensuring adequate environmental protection. This comes at a particularly concerning time, following recent judicial decisions that have already reduced federal water protections. By limiting review to narrowly defined “discharges” and constraining timelines and conditions, the rule undermines Congress’s clear intent that states and tribes serve as frontline protectors of water quality. Section 401 ensures that local expertise and community voices are not overridden by federal permitting decisions. Weakening this authority would disproportionately harm our communities and watershed health and make it harder to prevent pollution before it occurs. “Our duty to the whole, including to the unborn generations, bids us to restrain an unprincipled present-day minority from wasting the heritage of these unborn generations. The movement for the conservation of wildlife and the larger movement for the conservation of all our natural resources are essentially democratic in spirit, purpose and method.” -- Theodore Roosevelt This rollback is especially concerning for the Great Lakes and the Appalachian regions. The Great Lakes hold 20% of the world’s surface fresh water and supply drinking water to more than 40 million people. In Michigan, the proposal could directly affect decisions regarding Enbridge’s Line 5 oil pipeline, including a proposed tunnel and potential horizontal directional drilling beneath the Straits of Mackinac—an area of extraordinary ecological, cultural, and economic significance. Page 2 of 4 Enbridge has delayed a final decision on its Clean Water Act Section 404 permit from the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy. If the Environmental Protection Agency finalizes this rule, it could affect the outcome by restricting Michigan’s ability—and tribal nations’ treaty-protected authority—to fully evaluate and reject water quality risks. “A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise.” -- Aldo Leopold Appalachian rivers contain incredible biodiversity, providing habitat for more than half of all aquatic species in North America, and this biodiversity supports local economies and livelihoods. Fishing is an important part of Appalachian culture, with many people depending on it as a source of food. Meanwhile, the biodiversity of Appalachia draws people from all over, who come to recreate and experience its beauty. These visitors help to support local economies, which often have limited other sources of income. One study estimated that outdoor recreation in western North Carolina generated $4.9 billion in economic output and created 48,000 jobs. However, these economic benefits depend upon clean and healthy waterways that can continue to support the region’s biodiversity. Appalachian waterways also provide drinking water to more than 36 million people. Keeping these source waters clean is essential to ensuring that these people continue to have access to safe and affordable water. If these waters become contaminated, municipal water systems will be forced to implement greater water treatment, and the increased costs associated with this treatment will be passed on to customers, many of whom are already struggling to afford high utility bills. For Appalachians who get their water from private wells or mountain springs, the impacts will be even more dire. Since they do not benefit from municipal water treatment, they will be forced to choose between drinking contaminated water or relying on prohibitively expensive alternatives, like bottled water. Healthy waterways also help to protect Appalachian communities from the most severe impacts of flooding. Heavy rain events are becoming increasingly common in Appalachia, resulting in deadly and damaging flooding events, like those associated with Hurricane Helene. Natural waterways help to slow down the flow of water, reducing risks to both people and property during heavy rains. However, projects that interfere with natural waterways and the flow of water can disrupt their ability to mitigate flooding, making these conditions more dangerous and more expensive for Appalachian communities. Section 401 of the Clean Water Act gives states the authority to protect their waterways from both discharges of pollutants and other related harms. Under the proposed rule, the states’ authority under this section would be dramatically narrowed, making it harder for states to ensure their waters are protected. For example, a state would not be able to impose conditions on a project that alters downstream flows of water, even though such a project could result in dangerous and costly flooding in downstream communities. A state would also be limited in its ability to regulate indirect impacts to water quality, such as those associated with project construction, despite the fact that these impacts could result in contaminated drinking water and increased water costs for residents. Page 3 of 4 “Every man who appreciates the majesty and beauty of the wilderness and of wild life, should strike hands with the farsighted men who wish to preserve our material resources, in the effort to keep our forests and our game beasts, game-birds, and game- fish—indeed, all the living creatures of prairie and woodland and seashore—from wanton destruction. Above all, we should realize that the effort toward this end is essentially a democratic movement.” -- Theodore Roosevelt Water is a shared resource that sustains communities, ecosystems, and economies. Once contaminated, restoration can take generations. The current Section 401 authority provides essential safeguards that allow local communities to protect their water resources for current and future generations. We cannot give away more of our waters to industry while our communities, health, wildlife, and environment pay the price. States and tribes must retain the power to: • Consider cumulative and long-term water quality impacts • Protect treaty rights, fisheries, and drinking water • Deny certification when projects threaten water quality standards I strongly urge you to reconsider this proposed rule. By limiting the ability of states and tribes to ensure the protection of their waters, the proposed rule threatens to damage the environment, hurt the economy, and increase costs for everyone. The Great Lakes, Appalachian rivers, and all of our fresh water sources are too important to risk for the convenience of oil pipeline companies. Our nation’s waterways deserve comprehensive protection, not weakened standards that prioritize expedited project approvals over environmental stewardship. The Environmental Protection Agency should withdraw this proposal and instead strengthen, not weaken, Clean Water Act protections. If it won’t strengthen protections, the Environmental Protection Agency should at least maintain Section 401 of the Clean Water Act as it is currently written. “The ultimate test of a moral society is the kind of world that it leaves to its children.” -- Dietrich Bonhoeffer Thank you for your consideration of my comments. Please do NOT add my name to your mailing list. I will learn about future developments on this issue from other sources. Sincerely, Christopher Lish San Rafael, CA Page 4 of 4

comment_text:
I write to strongly oppose the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed rule to again improperly weaken regulations related to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (CWA or the Act). Section 401 represents an important tool used by states and Tribes to protect state and Tribal water resources from the impacts of federally permitted development. Section 401 is a linchpin of the cooperative federalism structure envisioned by Congress when it passed the Act in 1972 and is specifically designed to empower states and Tribes. The proposed rule would dramatically undercut the role provided to states and Tribes by the Act in protecting their waters.  The proposed rule largely recycles a rule issued in 2020 that upended almost fifty years of strong state and Tribal authority to ensure that projects such as dams, pipelines, highways, datacenters, and other projects are protective of state and Tribal waters and the important services they provide people and communities. In 2023 by a revised rule that restored the proper role for states and Tribes envisioned by the Act and the long-standing regulatory structure that stood in place since 1971. In doing so, it also updated the rule to clarify that state and Tribal reviews were appropriately limited to water related requirements and that there was a clear and timely process for applicants to follow.
 Of foremost concern, it would violate the Act by rejecting its clear meaning and overturning Supreme Court precedent confirming that meaning by limiting the scope of certification from the activity as a whole to the “discharge from a point source” of a project. This would dramatically limit the ability of states and Tribes to look at the totality of potential impacts and harms to waters from a project. 
 While this change is the most concerning provision of the proposed rule, there are several others that also unnecessarily and improperly seek to restrict the ability of states and Tribes to protect their waters. 
The 2023 rule also makes it clear that certification, conditions, and denial must regard water quality requirements. Moreover, the Section 401 process rarely results in the denial or undue delay of projects. For example, as EPA’s Economic Analysis shows, almost all permits issued by the Corps (which make up the overwhelming number of permits subject to Section 401) are either granted (95.5%) or waived (3.8%). Only 0.8% are denied.[JD2] 
 It also must be seen in relation to recent changes to the scope of Clean Water Act protections generally. Section 401 is only triggered when a federal permit or license involving a discharge to “waters of the United States” is at issue. In fact, most federal permits and licenses that trigger Section 401 are Section 404 discharge permits under the Clean Water Act itself. In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a decision in Sackett v. sEPA that dramatically reduced the number of waters covered by the federal Clean Water Act. Subsequently, this EPA is finalizing a rule that would even further limit the number of waters protected by the Act. If the proposed EPA rule governing “waters of the United States” is issued as proposed, it would result in an estimated 81% of historically federally protected wetlands lacking Clean Water Act protection[JD3] . Massive losses in protections under the Act for streams is also at issue. With these rollbacks, many projects will no longer need CWA permits, meaning that the trigger for Section 401 review for many projects will disappear altogether.

comment_text:
Subject: Protect Our Waters: Opposition to the Proposed 2026 EPA Rule Changes
To the EPA Review Board,

I am writing today not just as a concerned citizen, but as someone who believes that clean water is a fundamental right, not a luxury. The proposed 2026 rule changes to the Clean Water Act feel less like "streamlining" and more like a deliberate attempt to silence the people most affected by pollution: our States and Tribal nations.

The Clean Water Act was designed to empower locals, not sideline them. These proposed changes are a step backward for several critical reasons:

Erasing Tribal Sovereignty: These rules would effectively strip Tribes of their right to protect their own Reservation waters and object to permits that impact them. We should be honoring Tribal stewardship, not writing them out of the regulations.

Handcuffing Minnesota: In my home state, we rely on our current authority to protect world-class treasures like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. These rules would stop us from setting the necessary conditions to keep these waters "Exceptional."

A "Gift" to Polluters: Narrowing the scope of what we can review and forcing a "one-year waiver" is a recipe for disaster. If a company hides the truth about their environmental impact or if a natural disaster slows down a study, the EPA shouldn't reward them by letting the clock run out.

Unchecked Power: Giving the EPA Administrator the power to unilaterally decide that entire categories of waste—like mining or pipeline discharge—can bypass review is dangerous and unreasonable.

My research says The Clean Water Act was largely spurred into existence after the Cuyahoga River in Ohio literally caught fire for the 13th time in 1969. We have come too far since then to start dismantling the very tools that prevent us from returning to those days.

Also, here in Minnesota, we have roughly 11,842 lakes—that’s a lot of shoreline to protect, and we can’t do it if the EPA ties our hands.

The current rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting my family and my community than this proposed update ever could. I urge you to withdraw this proposal and keep the authority where it belongs: with the States and Tribes who actually live with the water.

Thank you for your time and for actually listening to the people on the ground.

Sincerely,
-Jeff Pollari

(this comment is on Docket ID # EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929)

There are too many serious risks involved with synthetic biology. This will come back to haunt us in more ways than one. One of my biggest concerns is contending with the different kinds of waste that will arise with this endeavor that may go unchecked straight into the environment. A freak accident for instance, could release harmful byproducts.

I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

comment_text: From: deb.shankland@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 1/29/2026 1:33:23 PM Subject: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 -------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from deb.shankland@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, I live in the Great Lakes watershed, specifically Lake Erie. I know well the history of a "nearly dead" Lake Erie, and the once terrible state of the Cuyahoga River, an Erie tributary. I witnessed and smelled the dead fish, the greasy sheen, and felt the shame of being part of "the Mistake on the Lake". Fortunately, I also witnessed and participated in the long recovery (over 50 years) of these waterbodies, thanks to the Clean Water Act (CWA). Now, both water bodies are the "places to be", fomenting thriving businesses along their banks, and adding to (instead of subtracting from) our health and quality of life. This is not the time to go back. In the last 50 years, there has been tremendous growth and development in my watershed and others in the Great Lakes region. This is not entirely positive: it has decreased green space and increased impervious surfaces. This makes protection of the little remaining green space, including wetlands and small tributary streams, imperative. Flooding is increasing due to global warming as well as the marked increase of impervious surfaces. The U.S. EPA should not only continue to enforce environmental laws and defend the CWA, but should actually INCREASE protections in order to protect our health and the economy by reducing flooding and pollution. The proposed rule change to Section 401 will instead weaken protections by removing control from states and Tribes. This is foolish and incredibly short-sighted. Further, this proposed rule change will strip protections of wetlands, which, for free, support recreational activities that bring in $50 billion annually to our region and filter pollutants, in addition to controlling flooding. Everyone, no matter their background or party affiliation, needs clean water and a functioning environment to survive. Everyone supports protections of our water resources, from intermittent streams to wetlands to our entire Great Lakes. Do not go backwards--it was awful. In support of our state and Tribal rights, I strongly urge you to fully enforce the CWA, strengthen it, and maintain the authority of states and Tribes to protect clean water. Sincerely, Debra Brecksville, OH

comment_text: From: annikafjelstad@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 2/9/2026 10:26:09 PM Subject: Docket ID# EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 — Opposition to Proposed 2026 Changes to Circumscribe Certification Authority of States and Tribes -------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from annikafjelstad@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, I strongly oppose the EPA’s proposed 2026 rule changes that would circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water. The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. The purpose of the EPA is to protect natural resources such as water, NOT to protect polluters. The people with the most at stake are the local states or tribal nations whose residents depend on the water for life. These people absolutely must maintain the ability to set standards for clean water. The EPA’s proposed 2026 certification rules are unlawful, unreasonable, and just plain wrong. Specifically: 1. ) I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations. 2. ) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. 3. ) I oppose all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water. 4. ) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 5. ) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish. Thank you for considering my comments, Sincerely, Annika Fjelstad 4436 Aldrich Ave S Minneapolis, MN 55419-4822 annikafjelstad@gmail.com

The Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM), as the state agency responsible for the daily implementation of the CWA water quality programs and the certifying authority for Section 401 water quality certifications in Indiana, is pleased to provide these comments in support of the proposed rule. IDEM previously provided feedback on EPA’s July 7, 2025, request for input on implementation challenges or regulatory uncertainty associated with the 2023 Rule at 90 Fed. Reg. 29828. As noted in that feedback, IDEM has effectively implemented the 2023 Rule, but noted areas where additional clarity may be appropriate. IDEM supports the revision and amendment to § 121.3, the scope of certification, and § 121.7, certification decisions. With respect to the revision made to § 121.3, IDEM agrees that “[t]he plain language of CWA section 401(a) directs states to certify that any discharge resulting from the proposed Federally licensed or permitted activity will comply with the enumerated provisions of the CWA.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 2023. As EPA points out, this interpretation is further supported by the revisions made in 1972 to CWA section 401, changing “activity” to “discharge.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 2024-25. As such, IDEM agrees that EPA’s interpretation is the best reading of Section 401. See Loper Bright v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 400 (2024). Additionally, IDEM is supportive of EPA requiring certifying authorities to include specific contents in all certification decisions with the amendments to § 121.7. Currently, IDEM’s certification conditions are within the appropriate scope, the language of which was successfully coordinated with Indiana’s three Corps Districts. The language used to support each condition includes legal citations to support conditions that are included to protect water quality. IDEM seeks clarity on a scenario in which our federal partners were to disagree and exclude a condition. Regarding the proposed changes to the Section 401(a)(2) process, IDEM is supportive of the proposed changes and is confident in its ability to comply. For coordination with neighboring jurisdictions, IDEM has previously successfully worked with Kentucky and reviewed and supported the conditions Kentucky required on projects proposing discharge of dredge and fill to the Ohio River. So far, all the projects, when permitted with the conditions in Kentucky’s 401 water quality certifications, comply with Indiana’s water quality standards. IDEM appreciates the opportunity to review these projects and believes the requirement to coordinate is not overly burdensome and will help streamline certifications. EPA has requested comment on the proposed contents of a request for certification under § 121.5. IDEM believes the proposed rule would help provide clear and specific guidance on what is needed to fulfill the proposed certification request. IDEM appreciates the opportunity to comment on EPA’s proposed rule “Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations.” IDEM supports EPA’s underlying rationale for reversing the 2023 Rule’s “activity as a whole” approach because Loper Bright requires that agencies adopt the “best reading” of the statute, rather than merely a “reasonable” reading under the Chevron deference doctrine. 91 Fed. Reg. at 2023. IDEM agrees with EPA that the 2023 Rule interpretation “does not reflect the best reading of the statute.” Id. In short, Loper Bright compels EPA to reevaluate whether its interpretation is the “best reading” of the statute, and the textual arguments set forth by EPA in the proposed rule support a discharge-focused approach. IDEM does not anticipate the revisions in the proposed rule to detract from its ability to maintain compliance. IDEM looks forward to continued collaboration on CWA implementation issues with EPA. Sincerely, Clint Woods Commissioner Indiana Department of Environmental Management

Reg. 2,008 (January 15, 2026). EEI generally supports the Proposed Rule, and in these comments offers modifications to further improve the certification process and facilitate the continued buildout of infrastructure required to meet American energy needs. EEI is the leading voice and advocate for investor-owned electric companies in the United States, which serve more than 250 million customers in 50 states and the District of Columbia. EEI member companies work every day to provide reliable energy to their customers at the lowest cost possible. EEI member companies also form the backbone of our nation’s electric power industry, which is essential to advancing our economic and national security priorities, including achieving global dominance in artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced computing technologies. Over the next five years, investor-owned electric companies will invest more than $1.1 trillion to enhance the electric grid, building critically needed new generation and transmission and distribution infrastructure required to power economic prosperity. EEI members own, operate, build, and maintain electric power generation, transmission, and distribution facilities requiring federal licenses or permits that deliver electric power throughout the U.S. These activities may result in discharges into navigable waters. EEI members are therefore directly impacted by the CWA Section 401 certification process and have a significant interest in its implementation. An efficient, consistent, and predictable certification process that simultaneously protects water quality is critical to EEI members’ goals of continuing to provide reliable energy at the lowest cost. Questions on these comments may be directed to Patrick McGuire (202-508-5167) or Daniel Whittle (202-508-5990). Sincerely, M. Patrick McGuire Associate General Counsel COMMENTS FROM THE EDISON ELECTRIC INSTITUTE ON THE U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY’S PROPOSED RULE, UPDATING WATER QUALITY CERTIFICATION REGULATIONS Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 February 17, 2026 The Edison Electric Institute (EEI) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA or Agency) proposed rule, Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations (Proposed Rule). 91 Fed. Reg. 2,008 (January 15, 2026). Through the Proposed Rule, EPA plans to update and clarify several substantive and procedural requirements for water quality certification under Clean Water Act (CWA or the Act) Section 401. EEI generally supports the Proposed Rule, and in these comments offers modifications to further improve the certification process and facilitate the continued buildout of infrastructure required to meet American energy needs. EEI is the leading voice and advocate for investor-owned electric companies in the United States, which serve more than 250 million customers in 50 states and the District of Columbia. EEI member companies work every day to provide reliable energy to their customers at the lowest cost possible. EEI member companies also form the backbone of our nation’s electric power industry, which is essential to advancing our economic and national security priorities, including achieving global dominance in artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced computing technologies. Over the next five years, investor-owned electric companies will invest more than $1.1 trillion to enhance the electric grid, building critically needed new generation and transmission and distribution infrastructure required to power economic prosperity. 1 CWA Section 401 grants states and Tribes that have been approved for “treatment as a state” status the authority to review activities requiring a federal license or permit that may result in a discharge into “navigable waters” to certify that any such discharge will comply with certain applicable federal, state, and tribal water quality requirements. See 33 U.S.C. § 1341(a). CWA Section 401 thus carves out an important water quality protection role for states and authorized Tribes in federal licensing and permitting processes. EEI members own, operate, build, and maintain electric power generation, transmission, and distribution facilities requiring federal licenses or permits that deliver electric power throughout the U.S. These activities may result in discharges into navigable waters. EEI members are therefore directly impacted by the CWA Section 401 certification process and have a significant interest in its implementation. An efficient, consistent, and predictable certification process that simultaneously protects water quality is critical to EEI members’ goals of continuing to provide reliable energy at the lowest cost. I. Electric Companies Are Investing to Meet Unprecedented Demand Growth. Across the country, investor-owned electric companies are investing in a broad range of technologies to deliver reliable power at the lowest reasonable cost to meet customers’ needs while also satisfying federal and state requirements. Though EEI member companies operate in differing regulatory environments and face varied customer demands, we share a clear message: to meet our nation’s needs in this moment, we must use every available tool to deploy new generation capacity and maximize the capabilities of our transmission and distribution infrastructure. 2 As EEI members drive to serve our customers at the lowest cost, customer needs are rapidly growing. The power sector is facing unprecedented levels of demand growth. Projections consistently show a significant amount of new generation capacity must come online in the years ahead, mostly due to increasing manufacturing and the rapid proliferation of AI and advanced computing technologies. This represents both a tremendous opportunity and a challenge for the power sector, after nearly two decades of minimal increases in net electricity demand and in the face of high development costs, supply chain and workforce pressures, affordability concerns for customers, and siting and permitting barriers. EEI members are well-positioned to meet this challenge and support this national priority, with plans for $1.1 trillion in grid investments during the next five years to better serve our customers and facilitate data center and major industrial development, while also achieving reliability and securing broader benefits for existing customers and communities. II. EEI Supports Finalization of EPA’s Clarification Regarding the Scope of Certification. EPA proposes to clarify that “[t]he scope of certification is limited to assuring that a discharge from a federally licensed or permitted activity will comply with applicable and appropriate water quality requirements.” 91 Fed. Reg. at 2,040 (to be codified at 40 C.F.R. § 121.3). Further, EPA proposed to define “discharge” as a “discharge from a point source into waters of the United States.” Id. (to be codified at 40 C.F.R. § 121.1). EEI supports finalizing this clarification. CWA Section 401(a)(1) states that the state licensing or permitting agency must certify that “any such discharge will comply with” applicable provisions of the CWA for any applicant for a federal license or permit to conduct any activity that “may result in any discharge into the navigable waters.” See 33 U.S.C. § 1341(a)(1). This section refers to the 3 importance of the discharge itself for a certification multiple times. Therefore, EPA’s clarification aligns the regulatory text with both the language and the intent of the CWA. III. EEI Supports Clarification of the One-Year Certification Timeframe. CWA Section 401 states that the certifying authority must act on a request for certification “within a reasonable period of time (which shall not exceed one year).” See 33 U.S.C. § 1341(a)(1). EEI members have experienced complications in multiple states regarding the one- year timeframe and therefore EEI supports EPA clarifying this timeframe in the Proposed Rule. Specifically, EEI supports EPA’s proposal to clarify that the timeline starts when the application is submitted; that resubmittal of additional information does not restart the timeline; and, that failure by the certifying authority to act on a request within the reasonable period of time results in a waiver. See 91 Fed. Reg. at 2,041. These clarifications provide certainty and predictability for EEI members throughout the country seeking certifications. EEI also supports EPA’s clarification that a certifying authority may not request withdrawal and resubmittal of a request for certification in order to extend the reasonable period of time. Id. (to be codified at 40 C.F.R. § 121.6(e)). EEI members have experienced the negative consequences of this approach in the past and support EPA providing clarification that authorities may no longer delay certification in this way. IV. EEI Supports the Uniformity and Certainty in the Proposed Rule Regarding the Required Elements of a Certification Request. EPA proposes to specify an enumerated list of documents and information that must be included in a request for certification for all Federal licenses or permits, and to remove regulatory text allowing states and tribes to require additional types of information in a request for certification. See 90 Fed. Reg. at 2,017 (to be codified at 40 C.F.R. § 121.5). EEI supports EPA providing uniformity and certainty across the country regarding the required elements of a 4 certification request. The certainty and predictability of a uniform request for certification will promote more efficient application processes for EEI members that operate across multiple states and tribal jurisdictions. It will allow members to file one unified application instead of multiple separate certification applications with different requirements across several jurisdictions, thereby streamlining the application process and speeding certification for projects that cross wide geographical ranges. V. EEI Supports EPA Clearly Defining a Role for Project Proponents Regarding Modifications of Certification Conditions. EPA proposes requiring the Federal agency, the certifying authority, and the applicant to all agree in writing that the certifying authority may modify a grant of certification (with or without conditions), before any modification occurs. See 90 Fed. Reg. at 2,041 (to be codified at 40 C.F.R. § 121.10). EEI supports this change for the same reason as the other proposed changes: it will provide certainty and predictability to applicants. In the past, EEI members have experienced circumstances where a certifying authority unilaterally pushes for impractical or unnecessary modifications to certification conditions. Requiring all parties to agree on modification will help ensure the modification is necessary and will lead to the best possible outcome for the application. VI. EPA Should Consider Exempting Facilities from CWA Section 401 Certification if the Facility already has a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Permit for the Relevant Discharges. In some instances, states have required CWA Section 401 certification where the facility in question has already established compliance with water quality requirements through an existing valid National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit issued pursuant to 5 Section 402 of the CWA by a state under delegated authority from EPA. 1 To the extent that a 401 certification is required for discharges to navigable waters or other applicable requirements included in the NPDES permitting process, EPA should clarify that a valid NPDES permit indicates compliance with water quality requirements under CWA Section 401. Indeed, a NPDES permit cannot be issued “when the imposition of conditions cannot ensure compliance with the applicable water quality requirements of all affected States,” or, for a new source, “if the discharge from its construction or operation will cause or contribute to the violation of water quality standards.” 2 This clarification will remove duplicative processes and therefore streamline compliance with the CWA. We emphasize that the limited role of Section 401 is demonstrated by the history of the provision as compared to that of Section 402, which created the CWA’s discharge permitting process. Prior to the passage of the modern CWA in 1972, Section 21(b) of the Water Quality Improvement Act contained a certification provision identical to Section 401, which applied to projects that did not proceed through a federally enforceable discharge permitting process, as that process did not yet exist. The Water Quality Improvement Act’s certification provision thus predated the development of the more comprehensive CWA permitting process under Section 402. Congress’ transference of the prior certification provision into Section 401 of the new CWA 1 These comments use “NPDES” to refer to CWA Section 402 permits issued by state authorities operating permitting programs under EPA delegated authority. Some states call these “SPDES” programs, the “S” standing for “State”, or insert the name of the state (“Texas Pollution Discharge Elimination System” or TPDES). These are state-issued permits that do not require a 401 certification. It is important to note that a CWA Section 402 permit issued by EPA itself, as for a non-delegated state, tribe, or territory, is a federally issued permit that must be supported by a 401 certification. 40 C.F.R. § 124.53(a). 2 40 C.F.R. § 122.4(d), (i). 6 in 1972, along with the creation of the NPDES process in Section 402, created two processes that should be read as not duplicative. Section 401 becomes duplicative, contrary to this statutory structure, when it is applied to projects that also must undergo Section 402 permitting. Congress’ inclusion of both Section 401 and the new Section 402 in the modern CWA creates a simple coordinated process. At its core, Section 401 is a pre-construction approval process, 3 whereas Section 402 permits are required for operations, not for construction. Section 401 also logically exists to apply pre-construction review to those projects to which the new Section 402 did not apply, just as it did prior to 1972 before the NPDES process existed— allowing the state to condition projects that otherwise will not undergo permitting. It is only rational that states would look to the Section 402 permitting process for continuing protection of water quality for projects whose operations result in a discharge. Therefore, based on the appropriate limited role of Section 401 in the overall CWA system, and given the requirement that, at least where discharges are concerned, NPDES permits must protect water quality standards, EPA should provide guidance to the states that: (1) the existence of a valid Section 402 permit provides reasonable assurance that the discharge will comply with water quality requirements, and (2) that this reasonable assurance creates a basis on which a 401 certification can be issued or, if the state prefers, waived. VII. EPA Should Revise the Pre-Filing Meeting Request Requirement. The Proposed Rule requires project proponents to request a pre-filing meeting from the certifying authority at least 30 days prior to a certification request submission. However, certifying authorities are allowed to waive or shorten this requirement. See 40 C.F.R. § 121.4. 3 See, e.g., § 401(a)(3), which explains that absent changed circumstances, permittees need not obtain a certification for operation when one has been obtained pre-construction. 7 In the experience of EEI members, the pre-filing meeting request requirement delays small projects that have minimal to no water quality impact. EEI members have noted that after a certifying authority receives a pre-filing meeting request for minor projects with minimal or no water quality impact, the certifying authority will then often wait the full 30 days before proceeding with the certification even if there are no other changes. As a result, the pre-filing requirement has become a de facto 30-day delay for small, short-lived, and generally non- controversial construction or maintenance projects. This type of delay is unnecessary, and the pre-filing meeting request process ends up slowing down certification with no concomitant benefit to the environment. EPA should instead make the pre-filing meeting request voluntary— or consider creating categorical exemptions from the requirement for smaller, less complex projects that have minimal or no water quality impacts, or need to be done on an emergency basis. At a minimum, EPA should consider allowing project proponents to participate in the certifying authority’s waiver process for determining whether the pre-filing meeting is necessary. These changes would provide flexibility and facilitate quicker certifications for the critical infrastructure projects EEI members conduct that have minimal or no water quality impacts. VIII. EPA Should Assert in Regulatory Text that Withdrawals from Navigable Waters Do Not Trigger the CWA Section 401 Process. Courts have concluded that a water withdrawal is not a discharge and therefore does not trigger the need for a water quality certification. 4 EPA appropriately clarified in the preamble to the 2023 rule that withdrawals from navigable waters neither trigger the CWA Section 401 4 See, e.g., North Carolina v. FERC, 112 F.3d 1175, 1187 (D.C. Cir. 1997) (holding that withdrawal of water from lake does not constitute discharge for CWA Section 401 purposes). 8 process, nor are they “discharges” whose impacts may be addressed by Section 401 certification conditions. 87 Fed. Reg. at 35,329. 5 Further, EPA appears to assert withdrawals from navigable waters do not trigger the CWA Section 401 process in the Proposed Rule by narrowing the scope of the certifying authority review to just an assessment of whether a facility’s point source discharges into waters of the United States comply with applicable water quality requirements, but does not explicitly exempt withdrawals from the certification process. 91 Fed. Reg. at 2,023. To provide clarity, the Agency should explicitly exempt withdrawals in the regulatory text. IX. Conclusion. EEI supports EPA’s finalization of the Proposed Rule with the modifications explained above. Questions on these comments may be directed to Patrick McGuire (202-508-5167) or Daniel Whittle (202-508-5990). 5 See also EPA, 2023 Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule Final 2023 Rule Questions & Answers (last updated Nov. 2024) at 6, https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-12/qa-for-2023-cwa-section-401-rule- implementation-112024.pdf. 9

comment_text:
I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

comment_text: Christopher Phalen Vice President, Domestic Policy February 17, 2026 The Honorable Jessica Kramer Assistant Administrator Office of Water Environmental Protection Agency 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, N.W. Washington, DC 20460 RE: Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations, 91 Fed. Reg. 2008 (January 15, 2026); Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 Dear Assistant Administrator Kramer: The National Association of Manufacturers (“NAM”) respectfully submits these comments on the proposed rulemaking issued by the Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA” or “the Agency”) entitled, Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations (“the proposed rule” or “the proposal”). The NAM appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule and supports the EPA’s commitment to recalibrating the implementation of Clean Water Act (“CWA”) Section 401 (33 U.S.C. 1341) to realign it with the best statutory reading and congressional intent of the CWA. The NAM is the voice of the manufacturing community and the leading advocate for a policy agenda that supports and empowers the 13 million people who make things in America. As the largest manufacturing association in the U.S., the NAM’s membership includes businesses of all sizes, across all industrial sectors, and in all 50 states. Manufacturers collectively contribute $2.9 trillion to the U.S. economy—and right-sized, commonsense regulations are critical to sustaining the manufacturing strength that underpins our nation’s prosperity. Manufacturers appreciate EPA’s commitment to delivering on the President’s directive to reconsider regulatory developments that present “substantial restraint[s] on our economic growth and ability to build and innovate,” 1 by proposing to “revise several procedural and substantive aspects of the Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule...to address areas of regulatory uncertainty and implementation challenges.”2 The NAM has long called for comprehensive permitting reform, inclusive of regulatory and legislative actions, to drive the growth and competitiveness of manufacturing in the U.S. Modernizing the implementing regulations of the CWA is a key part of such a comprehensive 1 Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation, Exec. Order No. 14192, 90 Fed. Reg. 9065 (6 February 2025); Presidential Memorandum: Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, Directing the Repeal of Unlawful Regulations (9 April 2025); Repeal of Greenhouse Gas Emissions Standards for Fossil Fuel-Fired Electric Generating Units, 90 Fed. Reg. 25752 (17 June 2025). RIN 2060-AW55; Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) and Nonattainment New Source Review (NNSR): Regulations Related to Project Emissions Accounting; Withdrawal of Proposed Rule, 90 Fed. Reg. 34206 (21 July 2025). RIN 2060-AV62. 2 Proposed rule, at 2008. 1 approach.3 And as the NAM stated in response to the Agency’s 2025 Establishment of Public Docket and Listening Sessions on Implementation Challenges Associated With Clean Water Act Section 401,4 “water quality certification under Section 401 of the CWA has posed challenges in instances when certifying authorities exceed the scope of their statutory mandate” 5 which has “impeded interstate commerce, to the detriment of energy development and manufacturing competitiveness.”6 Manufacturers in America need regulatory certainty and clarity to make capital-intensive investments in federally permitted facilities. Clear timelines and defined review criteria are critical for steel mills and raw material manufacturing and handling facilities that rely on predictable federal permitting schedules. The NAM therefore supports the Agency’s proposal and “a return to appropriate implementation of the requirements of Section 401 of the Clean Water Act, ensuring the certification process remains focused on point source discharges and not a project’s broader scope.”7 Rightsizing the Scope of Certification Reviews The NAM supports the Agency’s proposal to appropriately limit the scope of Section 401 certification reviews to “an assessment of whether a facility's point source discharges into waters of the United States will comply with specified water quality requirements.”8 This change from an activity-based scope is supported by the plain text of the CWA (as amended in 1972) and constitutes the best reading of the statute. See Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024). Focusing first on the statutory text of Section 401(a)(1), when read in its entirety, this section does not authorize a state or interstate water pollution control agency to provide a certification of an entire “activity.” 9 Rather, the term “activity” is used in a broader context wherein a state or interstate water quality certification is part of a larger “license or permit.” That certification is limited to “any discharge into the navigable waters” “at the point where the discharge originates or will originate” and ensures that “any such discharge will comply with the applicable provisions of sections 1311, 1312, 1313, 1316, and 1317 of this title.”10 The plain language of this subsection of the CWA demonstrates that the certification authority is not to be applied to an “activity” as a whole, only to point source discharges into the navigable waters (i.e., waters of the United States) that may result from any such activity. 3 America Builds: Clean Water Permitting and Project Delivery Hearing before Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, 119th Cong. (February 11, 2025) (statement of Noah Hanners, Executive Vice President, Nucor 4 Establishment of Public Docket and Listening Sessions on Implementation Challenges Associated With Clean Water Act Section 401. 90 Fed. Reg. 29828 (7 July 2025). Available at https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/07/07/2025-12564/establishment-of-public-docket-and-listening- sessions-on-implementation-challenges-associated-with 5 See NAM comments on Establishment of Public Docket and Listening Sessions on Implementation Challenges Associated With Clean Water Act Section 401. 90 Fed. Reg. 29828 (7 July 2025). Available at https://www.regulations.gov/comment/EPA-HQ-OW-2025-0272-0046 6 Ibid. 7 Ibid. 8 Proposed rule, at 2026 (emphasis in original). 9 33 U.S.C. 1341(a)(1) 10 33 U.S.C. 1341(a)(1) 2 This statutory interpretation is further supported by Loper Bright. Specifically, the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright obviates previous Chevron deference afforded by the Court to the Agency under its holding in PUD No. 1. of Jefferson County v. Washington Department of Ecology (PUD No. 1).11 The NAM discussed this case previously in our 2019 comments during the first Trump administration’s rulemaking process to right-size the implementation of CWA Section 401.12 As the Agency correctly lays out in the proposal, the Chevron deference afforded in PUD No. 1 was based on ”regulations that predated the 1972 CWA amendments and therefore contained outdated statutory terms, most importantly “activity” rather than “discharge” in CWA Section 401(a)(1).”13 The NAM supports the Agency’s proposal to limit the scope of certification reviews to properly align with statutory authority to “assur[e] that a discharge from a federally licensed or permitted activity will comply with applicable and appropriate water quality requirements.”14 This change will ensure there is no overreach into non-jurisdictional waters and provide much needed clarity for manufacturers by preventing Section 401 from being used to regulate activities unrelated to water quality impacts from the discharge. Certification Decisions Tied to Water Quality Standards Similar to constraining certification reviews to focus exclusively on point source discharges, the NAM also supports the Agency’s proposal to require certification conditions to cite the specific applicable water quality requirement. This will significantly enhance both transparency and enforceability while supporting consistent implementation across regional jurisdictions. As the NAM has noted since 2019, it is clear from the legislative history that Congress specifically intended to address water quality from point source discharges in Section 401 (as previously discussed). 15 Proposing to require state or interstate certifying authorities to expressly disclose if they are granting, granting with conditions, denying, or waiving a certification for an applicable license or permit, with additional supporting information required16 will provide a clear linkage between conditions and regulatory standards. This will help manufacturers understand compliance obligations and avoid conflicting requirements. The NAM therefore respectfully asks the Agency to finalize the proposed changes to CFR 121.7 (c)-(f). 11 511 U.S. 700 (1994). 12 Updating Regulations on Water Quality Certification, Proposed Rule, 84 Fed. Reg. 44,080 (Aug. 22, 2019). Available at https://www.regulations.gov/comment/EPA-HQ-OW-2019-0405-0878 13 Proposed rule, at 2025. 14 Proposed rule, at 2023. 15 See 2019 NAM comment, Available at https://www.regulations.gov/comment/EPA-HQ-OW-2019-0405-0878, pp. 3- 4, Senator Edmund Muskie quotation, etc. 16 In particular, where a certification is denied, ”where certification is denied, the EPA is proposing that the written notification of denial state the reasons for denial, including the specific water quality requirements with which the discharge(s) will not comply; a statement explaining why the discharge will not comply with the identified water quality requirements; or if the denial is due to insufficient information, a description of any missing water quality-related information.” 3 Standardizing Requests for Certification Along with ensuring that the scope of certifications are updated to reflect the correct statutory interpretation, manufacturers support the Agency’s proposal to standardize the contents of a certification request. The proposed changes will improve efficiency, consistency, and predictability in the certification process. Under the current regulatory regime, the process of merely requesting a Section 401 certification is too often used to delay and de facto block critical manufacturing and energy projects—before even reaching discharge and water quality analysis. A plain reading of the statute17 and controlling court precedent18 demonstrate that “receipt” does not require a certification request be “complete.” (Further discussion of manufacturers’ position on the Agency’s proposal regarding timelines is below). The process, beginning upon receipt of the certification request, is the forum through which completeness is to be achieved. Any other reading of the statute that allows sub-federal certifying authorities to impose differing or subjective criteria of “completeness” would obviate the authority granted to the Administrator of the Agency under the CWA. 19 The Agency, in its proposed changes to CFR 121.5 eliminating state- or tribe-specific additional information requirements, provides clear guidelines as to what constitutes a “complete” application upon “receipt.” The NAM supports these proposed revisions, as they will reduce inconsistent practices across jurisdictions affecting permittees, while lowering administrative burden without diminishing water quality protection. To augment the Agency’s proposal in CFR 121.5, the NAM also respectfully requests additional clarification that the standardized list of required materials in 121.5 is intended to be sufficient for certification review and that completeness determinations may not be used to expand the scope of review or delay the start of the statutory review period, including by relying on open-ended language such as “other relevant documentation” in the proposed 121.5(c)(4). Ensuring Appropriate Timelines Returning to the issue of the timeline afforded to certifying authorities to grant, deny, or waive certification, the NAM supports the Agency’s proposal. Firm deadlines are particularly important for major projects subject to Section 401. The statute is clear that, “[i]f the State, interstate agency, or Administrator, as the case may be, fails or refuses to act on a request for certification, within a reasonable period of time (which shall not exceed one year) after receipt of such request, the certification requirements of this subsection shall be waived with respect to such Federal application.”20 The proposal appropriately reinforces the statutory one-year maximum period for action on a certification request. Additionally, removing automatic extensions tied to public notice or force majeure events promotes timely decision-making. The NAM appreciates the Agency proposing 17 33 U.S.C. 1341(a)(1) 18 New York State Department of Environmental Conservation v. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 884 F.3d 450 (2d Cir. 2018) 19 “The Administrator is authorized to prescribe such regulations as are necessary to carry out his functions under this chapter.” 33 U.S.C. 1361(a). 20 U.S.C. 1341(a)(1), emphasis added 4 to bar certifying authorities from requesting or compelling applicants to withdraw a request for certification to avoid exceeding the clear one-year statutory requirement. Protecting Applicant Rights in Certification Modifications Manufacturers recognize that some modifications to certifications, or modifications made in the certifying process, are necessary and provide value to projects and water quality outcomes. The current regulations implementing Section 401, however, do not include the project applicant as a formal part of any agreement to proceed with a modification or the final language of such a modification. This has too often led to a lack of trust between certifying authorities and applicants, when applicants ultimately must effectuate any certification modification. It has also proven to be a mechanism by which certifying authorities can misuse the modification process to impose unreasonable modifications on an applicant, in some cases providing de facto certification denials without an authority having to formally deny a project certification as the CWA requires. The NAM therefore supports the Agency’s proposed revisions to CFR 121.10 clarifying the procedures for modifying an issued Section 401 water quality certification. Specifically, providing a defined process for applicant involvement in certification modifications promotes transparency, fairness, and better coordination between applicants and certifying authorities. Additionally, maintaining the prohibition on unilateral modification of certifications by certifying authorities and allowing applicant participation during the modification process will improve predictability for all stakeholders. Providing Predictable Neighboring State Review and Objection Process Finally, regarding the CWA Section 401(a)(2), which prescribes how the Agency notifies “other State[s]” (currently referred to in the CFR as “neighboring jurisdictions”) of potential water quality impacts from a proposed certification in a different state, the NAM supports the proposed rule establishing a 90-day deadline for federal agencies to act on neighboring state objections. This will reduce the open-ended delay risk and ensure the predictable resolution of other states’ objections, which is vital for major projects. The NAM agrees and supports the Agency’s determination that the proposed firm deadlines preserve neighboring state participation while safeguarding timely project decisions. ******** The NAM appreciates the Agency’s consideration of these comments and the Administration’s ongoing engagement with manufacturers throughout the process of preparing this proposal to correctly implement the requirements of CWA Section 401. Manufacturers strongly support a return to appropriately scoped and timed certifications that provide certainty and predictability to manufacturers while reflecting the appropriate balance between federal and state authorities, as Congress intended. Sincerely, Christopher Phalen Vice President, Domestic Policy 5

comment_text: From: stephaniejhemphill@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 2/10/2026 11:27:08 AM Subject: Docket ID# EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 — Opposition to Proposed 2026 Changes to Circumscribe Certification Authority of States and Tribes -------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from stephaniejhemphill@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, I wish to communicate my strong opposition to the EPA’s proposed 2026 rule changes that would limit certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water. The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. These proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. 1. ) Near me, the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa has done pioneering and effective work to protect the water quality in the St. Louis River. They rely on federal support, and the federal government has a trust responsibility to help them. Therefore, I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. 2. ) In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. Therefore, I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” 3. ) It is a mistake to tighten a noose around the scope of certification. The proposed rules would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water. We have a lot of experience with this in the Minnesota mining country. 4. ) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 5. ) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish. Thank you for considering my comments, Sincerely, Stephanie Hemphill 3614 Prindle Rd. Duluth MN 55803 Sincerely, Stephanie Hemphill 3614 Prindle Rd Duluth, MN 55803-9340 stephaniejhemphill@outlook.com

comment_text:
I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

I strongly support increased transparency in property broker transactions as a necessary step toward fairness and accountability in the trucking industry. For too long, motor carriers and owner-operators have operated with limited visibility into brokered transactions, often resulting in disputes over payments and a lack of trust in the system.

By requiring brokers to disclose transaction records promptly and in an accessible format, FMCSA will create a more level playing field, ensuring that carriers receive fair compensation and can make informed business decisions. Transparency will deter unethical practices, improve industry stability, and promote fair competition.

I urge FMCSA to adopt strong enforcement measures to ensure compliance with these transparency rules. Without meaningful penalties for non-compliance, brokers may continue opaque practices that disadvantage carriers.
