comment_text:
I hope this letter finds you well. I am writing to express my concerns regarding the lack of support for owner operators in enforcing their rights under Rule 49 CFR 371.3. As a stakeholder in the trucking industry, I believe it is crucial for the FMCSA to actively assist and advocate for the rights of owner operators. FMCSA has allowed broker fraud and non-compliance to run rampant and has yet to create the comprehensive enforcement program.

The lack of understanding by the FMCSA concerning this issue is astounding. It is imperative to comprehend that unlawful brokerage activities have far-reaching consequences. When brokers operate without proper oversight, it affects carriers' ability to maintain safe equipment, afford required insurance policies, and comply with licensing and permit requirements. These issues directly impact highway safety and the integrity of our nation's transportation infrastructure.

 Proper enforcement of rules deters unethical practices and enhances safety. The FMCSA must enforce regulations to protect the supply chain's integrity and the trucking industry's operational safety. The current process & lack of enforcement has led to high levels of fraud, predatory practices, and all stakeholders involved suffering. The industry is being exploited and is vulnerable as a result. 

The FMCSA has provided no way to report general freight brokers non-compliance. As a result the integrity & safety of the general freight industry is severely compromised. 

As the industry has evolved, so has the increase of identity theft, fraud, and market manipulation. This necessitates the dire need for regulation & oversight of load boards requirements, record keeping, privacy policies, data sharing, security, rate reporting, and data collection. At this time, there is zero oversight & enforcement upon general freight brokers. 

While we support strengthening the agency's teeth to better enforce the law and rules and regulations against brokers, we wish to point out that FMCSA already has enough teeth to immediately and diligently take a bite out of broker abuse with regards to CFR 371.3.  We respectfully request that they do so at this time.  

We urge Congress to support the FMCSA in these efforts and, if necessary, provide additional legislative clarity to empower the agency to carry out its duties effectively in these specific issues. Your attention to this matter is crucial in upholding the integrity and safety of our nation’s transportation system. 

Respectfully,

comment_text: From: eplmeyer@everyactioncustom.com To: OW-Docket <OW-Docket@epa.gov> Date: 2/10/2026 10:37:19 AM Subject: Docket ID# EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 — Opposition to Proposed 2026 Changes to Circumscribe Certification Authority of States and Tribes -------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------- [You don't often get email from eplmeyer@everyactioncustom.com. Learn why this is important at https://aka.ms/LearnAboutSenderIdentification ] Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open attachments or click on provided links. Dear Administrator Lee Zeldin, I appreciate the opportunity to communicate my strong opposition to the EPA’s proposed 2026 rule changes that would circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water. The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. The EPA’s proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. The EPA’s proposed 2026 certification rules are unlawful, unreasonable, and just plain wrong. Specifically: 1. ) I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations. 2. ) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park. 3. ) I oppose all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water. 4. ) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 5. ) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish. Thank you for considering my comments, Sincerely, Ms. Emily Meyer 4109 Chowen Ave S Minneapolis, MN 55410-1015 eplmeyer@gmail.com

Dear Sir/Madam: When I worked at NOAA Fisheries Northeast Fisheries Science Center Woods Hole Laboratory, I participated in the Waquoit Bay Watershed Ecological Risk Assessment project which focused on stressors (Climate change; nutrient pollution; overfishing and toxic chemical contamination) on wild places, wild things. In modern times one would add environmental justice and affordable/attainable housing as socioeconomic factors in this Cape Cod watershed where my church is located. I spent over 40 years as an environmental activist at the Superfund/Safe Drinking Water Act cleanup at Joint Base Cape Cod which has expended $1.3 billion on the cleanup of groundwater/protection of of the Upper Cape Cod Water Supply Reserve (our future drinking water supply). The fish and shellfish in local rivers/ponds is contaminated with PFAS chemicals at levels of concern for Mashpee Wampanoag Tribal members and freshwater anglers seeking food to put food on the table (based on monitoring by University of Rhode Island Sources, Transport, Exposure and Effects of PFAS). I used to be the Recreational Fisheries Coordinator in the Northeast. JBCC is on state land and they utilize the Massa. Department of Environmental Protection PFAS 6 (20 parts per trillion) as the maximum contaminant level for the SDWA cleanup (Which is still in process for PFAS contaminants). Governor Healy turned down Congressionally allocated funds for the Massa. Army National Guard Multipurpose Machine Gun Range because off the slow progress of the Air Force Civil Engineering Center SDWA/CERCLA cleanup. She is awaiting the US EPA Regon 1 report on the PFAS cleanup The proposed US EPA for section 401 of the Clean Water Act which limits state and indigenous government review of Clean Water Act projects is likely to generate similar opposition and delays in various clean water projects and cleanups due to law suits/Congressional legislation. comment_text: February 17, 2026 Submitted via: http://www.regulations.gov U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, EPA Docket Center, Water Docket, Mail Code 28221T 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW Washington, DC 20460 Re: Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 – Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations Dear Madam or Sir: The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (The Alliance) strongly supports the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) proposed rule published on January 15, 2026, regarding Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929 – Updating the Water Quality Certification (WQC) Regulations (Proposed Rule). The Alliance provides the following comments and recommendations for your consideration. The Alliance is the largest oil and gas trade association in the Mid-Continent and the only trade association in Oklahoma to represent all sectors of the state’s oil and natural gas industry. Representing more than 1,700 individuals and member companies, the Alliance’s membership includes oil and natural gas producers, service providers to the oil and natural gas industry, midstream companies, refiners, and other associated businesses. Our members include companies of all sizes, ranging from small, family- owned companies to large, publicly traded corporations. Our members are responsible for 83% of all operated crude oil and natural gas production in Oklahoma. When non-operated production is considered, we estimate our members produce, transport, process, and refine more than 97% of Oklahoma’s crude oil and natural gas. Additionally, our members have operations, assets, or interests in most of the United States’ oil and natural gas producing regions as well as internationally. Our members develop private, state, and federal minerals and operate on federal lands in Oklahoma and in other states. The Proposed Rule is important to our members, especially those with large linear projects that cross multiple states that require a federal permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act (CWA). Some states have delayed or denied such permits for a myriad of issues unrelated to water quality. The Proposed Rule Increases Transparency, Efficiency, and Predictability for Section 401 Certifications. EPA’s Proposed Rule is a vital step toward restoring the rule of law and providing the regulatory certainty required for long-term capital investment for large infrastructure projects. The Proposed Rule balances the scope of the CWA Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule (2023 Rule) to 500 N.E. 4th Street, Oklahoma City, OK 73104 405-942-2334 www.thepetroleumalliance.com 1 provide greater regulatory certainty for applicants to receive their WQCs for projects while protecting waters of the U.S. The Proposed Rule aligns the regulations with the best reading of the CWA Section 401 and the legislative history, increases transparency, efficiency, and predictability for certifying authorities and the regulated community, and ensures that States and authorized Tribes understand and adhere to their Section 401 role. Among the many proposed revisions supported by The Alliance, the Proposed Rule better aligns the regulation with the law, focuses on the “discharges” rather than the “activity”, appropriately and reasonably aligns Section 401 certifications with the purpose of the CWA, establishes a "reasonable period of time" for state review (i.e., not to exceed one year in accordance with the law), clarifies when and how the 1-year clock for certification is started, limits the certifying authorities request for additional information not related to the discharge, identifies specific content in certification decisions and explanation of certification conditions, prohibits states from requesting an applicant to withdraw and resubmit a request for certification, eliminates automatic extensions, and removes Section 121.11 and instead appropriately directs Tribes to utilize the existing regulations at 40 CFR 131.8 if they are interested in pursuing treatment in a similar manner as a State for CWA Section 401. Recommendations to Enhance Clarity, Predictability and Consistency of the Proposed Rule 1. Information or Conditions Exceeding Section 401. If a state requests information from an applicant or imposes conditions in a WQC that exceed (i.e., is outside) the scope of the Section 401 identified in the Proposed Rule, applicants would have to remedy the issue in court. This means litigation of both the Proposed Rule and individual WQC is likely to continue. EPA is responsible for developing regulations and guidance to ensure effective implementation of CWA Section 401. To minimize or avoid unnecessary litigation, we request EPA include text in the final rule that provides an illustrative list of prohibited non-water quality information or conditions exceeding (i.e., are outside the scope) Section 401, and explicitly prohibit requests or allow conditions that are non-water quality related in the final rule. 2. Extension of the Reasonable Period of Time. Section 121.6(d) states that, [t]he Federal agency and certifying authority may agree in writing to extend the reasonable period of time for any reason (emphasis added), provided that the extension shall not cause the reasonable period of time to exceed one year from the date that the request for certification was received.” We support this statement except for the inclusion of “any reason” as it could be used as a tactic to delay a WQC up to the 1-year statutory limit unnecessarily. Such extensions should only be considered where the certifying authority has provided a credible justification regarding a significant issue related to the project discharge, not just “any reason” and without any justification. In addition, the applicant should be provided notice and justification of the extension. As such, we request EPA include language in the final rule that requires the certifying authority provide credible justifications for an extension of the reasonable period of time that are substantial to the project discharge to ensure the process is not unreasonably delayed. Additional text should be included in the final rule requiring the justification and notice of the extension to be provided to the applicant. 3. Modification. We support the inclusion of language “that the Federal agency, the certifying authority, and applicant agree in writing that the certifying authority may modify a grant of certification (with or without conditions), the certifying authority may modify only the agreed-upon portions of the certification” and that “[t]he certifying authority is required to 500 N.E. 4th Street, Oklahoma City, OK 73104 405-942-2334 www.thepetroleumalliance.com 2 obtain the applicant’s agreement on the language of the modification.” However, the proposed revisions do not identify the level of significance in which a modification can be considered and/or initiated. For example, modifications should only be considered where there is a "significant change" in the discharge, i.e., one that materially increases the volume or changes the chemical nature of the discharge. Minor design revisions that do not affect the “discharge” should not result in a modification. We request EPA include language in the final rule to address that a modification can only be considered and/or initiated when there is a significant change in the discharge. 4. Enforcement. The Proposed Rule does not provide clarity on what entity conducts compliance inspections and enforcement actions. This creates significant regulatory uncertainty for our members. Since a specific Federal agency issues a permit, it is only reasonable and appropriate for that Federal agency to conduct compliance inspections and enforcement. Otherwise, having multiple entities [state(s) and the Federal agency] conducting compliance inspections and enforcement will only lead to regulatory uncertainty and inconsistent inspections and enforcement, especially if there are multiple certifying authorities involved. As such, we request EPA add language to the final rule that the authority for compliance inspections and enforcement actions lies with the Federal agency issuing the permit. 5. “Other State”. Under Section 121.14(d), “[t]he Federal agency shall consider recommendations from the notified other State and the Administrator, and any additional evidence presented to the Federal agency at the hearing, and determine whether additional Federal license or permit conditions may be necessary to ensure that any discharge from the project will comply with the other State’s water quality requirements. If such conditions may be necessary, the Federal agency shall include them in the Federal license or permit.” However, this provision does not provide a timeframe in which the Federal agency makes this determination. We request EPA include text in the final rule that requires the Federal agency to make this determination as soon as possible, but no later than 30 days ensuring that the determination does not exceed the statutory 1-year certification time frame. Conclusion The Section 401 certification process must be transparent, predictable, and grounded in the law. By streamlining the certification process, it allows our industry to more efficiently plan and construct critical infrastructure required to provide Americans with affordable, reliable energy. This not only lowers costs for American consumers but also strengthens our ability to support our allies abroad. The Alliance requests EPA move quickly to finalize the Proposed Rule. We appreciate your consideration of the above comments and recommendations to enhance regulatory certainty of the final rule. If you have any questions, please contact me at 405-601-2124. Sincerely, Angie Burckhalter Sr. V.P. of Regulatory and Environmental Affairs 500 N.E. 4th Street, Oklahoma City, OK 73104 405-942-2334 www.thepetroleumalliance.com 3

comment_text:
I am writing to formally submit my concerns regarding the regulatory approval and labeling of the beetroot red color additive produced by Phytolon. While the resulting pigment may be chemically similar to that found in traditional beets, the method of production and the proposed marketing of this ingredient as "natural" raise significant safety, transparency, and allergenicity concerns that have not been sufficiently addressed.

1. Misleading "Natural" Characterization
The characterization of this additive as a "natural" color is fundamentally misleading to the consumer. This dye is not "sourced from nature" in the traditional sense; it is a product of Synthetic Biology (SynBio), synthesized in industrial fermentation vats using genetically engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Consumer Deception: Consumers associate "beetroot red" with a whole-food source. Labeling a vat-grown, bio-engineered pigment as "natural" or "beetroot-derived" obscures the reality of its synthetic origin.

2. Concerns Regarding Synthetic Biology and Process Integrity
The use of multi-gene biosynthetic pathways (including genes like BvDODA1 and BvCYP76AD1) inserted into a yeast host represents a high degree of processing. This is a radical departure from simple extraction.

The stability of these engineered pathways over long-term industrial cycles and the potential for unintended metabolic byproducts must be scrutinized more heavily than traditional food colors.

3. Unaddressed Allergenicity and Residual Contamination
The safety profile of this additive is inextricably linked to its production host. Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae introduces specific risks that are not present in soil-grown beets:

Residual Host Cell Proteins (HCPs): Even with high-level purification, there is a risk of residual yeast proteins remaining in the final dye. For individuals with yeast allergies or sensitivities, this poses a direct health risk.

Novel Protein Exposure: The presence of biosynthetic enzymes (such as the glucosyltransferases used to stabilize the dye) has not been sufficiently evaluated for potential allergenicity in the human gut or the impact on the microbiome.

Lack of Long-Term Data: There is a dearth of independent, peer-reviewed, long-term feeding studies that confirm the safety of these specific fermented betalains compared to their traditionally extracted counterparts.

4. Call for Rigorous Safety Testing
Before final approval is granted, the following must be mandated:

1. Proteomic Analysis: Rigorous testing to prove the absolute absence of residual yeast DNA and allergenic proteins.

2. Clear Labeling Standards: Strict enforcement of labeling that prevents the use of "natural" or "no artificial colors" for any ingredient produced via Synthetic Biology.

3. Allergen Warnings: Mandatory disclosure if the product was manufactured using a yeast-based fermentation process, to protect sensitive populations.

Conclusion: The push for "sustainable" colors should not come at the expense of consumer transparency and safety. The agency must prioritize the "Right to Know" for consumers who wish to avoid Synthetic Biology and ensure that the allergen screening for these novel additives is as rigorous as those for pharmaceutical-grade biologics. I urge the agency to require clear labeling that distinguishes between plant-extracted pigments and those produced via Synthetic Biology.

comment_text:
I am a groundwater geologist with professional experience evaluating surface water–groundwater interactions and stream and river habitats. I submit this comment to express concern that the proposed revisions to 40 CFR Part 121 would significantly weaken protection of waters of the United States by limiting Clean Water Act Section 401 certification to point-source discharges alone.

Streams and rivers are fragile, interconnected systems in which degradation frequently occurs through hydrologic alteration, physical habitat modification, wetland and floodplain disconnection, and cumulative impacts rather than through exceedances of discharge-based pollutant criteria. Restricting Section 401 certification to discharges would prevent states and tribes from addressing these dominant mechanisms of impairment and from ensuring compliance with water quality standards designed to protect aquatic life.

Please see the attached comment for a detailed technical discussion and recommendations to ensure that Section 401 certification remains an effective tool for protecting water quality standards and the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of waters of the United States.

comment_text:
February 6, 2026

Ms. Lauren Kasparek
Oceans, Wetlands, and Communities Division 
Office of Water (4504-T) 
Environmental Protection Agency 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20460 

Attention: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929, “Updated the Water Quality Certification Regulations” 

Re: Comment Deadline Extension Request 

Dear Ms. Kasparek,
The Skokomish Indian Tribe submits this letter to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in response to the agencies’ request for written feedback on the proposal titled “Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations,” published in the federal register on January 15, 2026. 

The federal register notice, unfortunately, identifies a very short comment period that does not adequately support tribal engagement or the required tribal consultation that are necessary procedural steps when considering this level of agency action. For this reason, The Skokomish Indian Tribe is formally requesting an extension of the current February 17, 2026 comment deadline.

Tribes have a substantial interest in the proposed rule and implementation and need more time to provide meaningful feedback. The federal government’s trustee obligations to protect treaty-reserved rights and resources, and the years-long dialogue about how to properly implement the Clean Water Act in a manner consistent with federal trust obligations, is symptomatic of the need to extend the comment period beyond the prescribed 30 days. comment_text:
My Name is Marissa Neal. I am submitting this comment as a concerned Texas resident who is passionate about promoting clean water and protecting our environment. I am concerned that the EPA’s proposed limitation on Clean Water Act Section 401 certification for point-source discharges into WOTUS, combined with stricter limits on the reasonable period for state review, would disproportionately harm environmental justice communities and weaken protections for wildlife and interconnected water systems. With Texas operating under a more limited pre-2015 WOTUS framework, many waters that support fish, birds, wetlands, and communities, such as small streams, flood-connected waterways, and groundwater systems, are already excluded from federal jurisdiction. Further narrowing the scope of waters that can be considered for discharge impacts under Section 401 risks allowing pollution to affect these connected systems without adequate review or accountability. 
Discharges from industrial facilities, ports, pipelines, and stormwater infrastructure often affect non-WOTUS waters before impacts even reach federally regulated waters, causing direct harm to habitats, wildlife, and communities. Limiting what states may consider and how much time they are given to review applications undermines Section 401’s role as an environmental justice safeguard. Having a constrained “reasonable period of time” can pressure certifying authorities to rush decisions or overlook cumulative and indirect impacts, shifting environmental and public health risks onto vulnerable ecosystems. EPA should retain sufficient flexibility in both scope and timing to allow states and tribes to fully assess water quality impacts reasonably related to licensed discharge, consistent with the Clean Water Act’s goal of protecting the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters. 

Sincerely, 
Marissa Neal

comment_text:
Administrator Lee Zeldin and Lauren Kasparek
United States Environmental Protection Agency
Oceans, Wetlands, and Communities Division, Office of Water (4504-T)
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20460
 
RE: Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification Improvement Rule
 
Dear Administrator Zeldin,
I write on behalf of Owámniyomni Okhódayapi, a Dakota-led nonprofit based in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in response to the Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act Section 401 water quality certification regulations. We respectfully urge the EPA not to adopt the proposed rule, as it would undermine state and tribal authority to safeguard waters essential to our communities, cultures and public health.
Owámniyomni Okhódayapi is leading the cultural and environmental restoration of a five-acre site on the Mississippi Riverfront at Owámniyomni, a place of cultural, spiritual and ecological significance for the Dakota people – Native Americans whose ancestral homelands are what is now known as Minnesota. Once a thriving gathering place, Owámniyomni (or St. Anthony Falls) was severely damaged by decades of industrialization. The falls collapsed due to tunneling and other milling impacts, the water was polluted and critical habitat destroyed. We work collaboratively with the four Dakota Nations in Minnesota to amplify their voices and visions including to improve water quality and restore habitats central to our heritage. 
Central to Dakota values is the understanding that water is a living relative with inherent rights, deserving of care and protection. This responsibility compels us to oppose policies that make it easier to pollute or harder for communities to prevent harm.
The Clean Water Act has long served as the nation’s strongest framework for protecting rivers, streams, wetlands and drinking water sources. A pillar of that framework is Section 401, which affirms the authority of states and authorizes tribes to review federally permitted projects to ensure they do not impact local water quality. This authority reflects the Act’s recognition that states and tribes are best positioned to evaluate local conditions, cumulative impacts and community needs.
Diluting state and tribal authority under Section 401 puts water quality at risk for millions of people and disproportionately harms Native communities already burdened by the impacts of pollution by industrialization and commercialization.
We are also concerned that this proposal continues the current administration’s rollback of Clean Water Act protections, which was designed to fast-track projects and reduce costs for developers at the expense of water quality safeguards. The EPA has provided no evidence that Section 401 authority has been misused or that a regulatory overhaul is necessary. In other words, we believe the proposed rule fails to demonstrate a problem and instead would make it easier for industries to pollute waterways without proper accountability.
We urge the EPA to withdraw its proposed Section 401 rule to fully preserve state and tribal authority under the Clean Water Act and protect water as the living relative it is.

Sincerely,
Shelley Buck
President
Owámniyomni Okhódayapi

comment_text:
Lauren Kasparek
Oceans, Wetlands, and Communities Division
Office of Water (4504-T)
Environmental Protection Agency
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20460

Attention: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929, “Updated the Water Quality Certification Regulations”

Dear Ms. Kasparek,

The proposed updates to section 401 of the Clean Water Act would remove comprehensive water quality assurance to the overall project. Because the proposal focuses on the point source discharge and not the entire body of water, the health of smaller streams, wetlands, and headwaters are at risk. The proposed rule also limits state and tribal power to regulate federally-permitted projects despite the potential effect of the projects’ impacts on the bodies of water. 

Reverting to the 2020 update to Section 401 that limits state and tribal authority of conditions to certifications will likely degrade our nation’s water quality and ultimately the health of our environment and communities.The unusually short window for public comment should be extended by 90 days to give the necessary and appropriate stakeholders to weigh in on the issue. 

I strongly urge the EPA to extend the period for public comment and seriously consider denying the proposed rule. 

Best,
E Williams

display_name: Northwest Colorado Council of Gov'ts Water Quality/ Quantity Committee (QQ)
comment_text:
Please find attached comments from the Northwest Colorado Council of Governments Water Quality/Quantity Committee (“QQ”), which is the only group of local governments in Colorado dedicated to protecting the headwaters of the Colorado River basin, including the headwaters of the Colorado, Blue, Eagle, Roaring Fork, Yampa, and Gunnison Basins (“Headwaters Region”). 

QQ respectfully requests that the EPA abandon its efforts to revise the Proposed Rule to reinstate the long-standing cooperative federalism practices in the Clean Water Act and specifically in Section 401.

rationales.actionability: The request to 'abandon' the revision effort is clear, but it is not very nuanced or feasible as a regulatory recommendation. It does not offer alternative language, targeted changes, or specific procedural requests.
rationales.structure_formatting: The comment is concise, readable, and professionally phrased. It is brief and organized into a short introduction and a request, though it lacks substantive structure beyond that.

overall_summary: The comment is directly relevant and professionally written, but it is extremely brief and largely unsupported. It states a clear position against the proposed section 401 revisions, yet provides minimal reasoning, evidence, or actionable alternatives.

display_name: State of Utah Public Lands Policy Coordinating Office
comment_text:
The State of Utah (State) supports the administration’s attempt to improve the clarity, consistency, and effectiveness of certification and appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 401 Water Quality Certification. Section 401 has long served as an essential mechanism for safeguarding Utah’s waters. Utah urges the EPA to implement any changes in 401 Certification through the framework of cooperative federalism, ensuring that the State retains its authority to regulate and protect its resources. Preserving Utah’s sovereign interests and the right to manage its own resources is critical to shielding the State from potential federal overreach by less supportive administrations.
Utah faces unique water resource challenges. Our state is experiencing a persistent historic drought, coupled with rapid population growth and significant public land holdings. These stressors place extraordinary pressure on Utah’s water supply and underscore the need for a regulatory framework that empowers states to manage water quality effectively. A rule that respects state sovereignty and promotes clarity and predictability is essential to ensuring sustainable water management in the West.
In addition, Utah recently submitted comments emphasizing the importance of defining “waters of the United States” (WOTUS) consistent with the Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett v. EPA . The Sackett standard requires clear, objective criteria for the exercise of jurisdiction over states’ resources. As the EPA considers revisions to Section 401, Utah urges the agency to recognize that “[r]egulation of land and water use lies at the core of traditional state authority.” Utah appreciates federal efforts to improve the efficiency, clarity, and consistency of Section 401 certifications and requests that these efforts be implemented in a way that respects the State’s role as the primary regulator of its own resources.
In this spirit of cooperative federalism and state sovereignty, Utah highlights Congress’s intention to recognize the State as primary in regulating water resources. Specifically, Congress expressly recognized “the primary responsibilities and rights of states to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution” and “to plan the development and use… of land and water resources.” Section 1370 further provides that, except as expressly stated, nothing in the Act shall impair state jurisdiction over waters within its borders . These provisions confirm that states are the primary stewards of water quality within their boundaries.
Accordingly, Utah asks the EPA to maintain the State’s right to request and evaluate additional information when processing a 401 Certification . As noted in the Federal Register, a request for Certification “may not necessarily represent the totality of information a certifying authority may need to act on a request.” Id. The states’ ability to request additional information enables the states to protect water resources and avoid denying Certifications when the “request for certification” lacks essential information needed for compliance. Further, Utah requests that the EPA respect the state’s authority to deny requests for incompleteness if additional information is not provided within the statutory maximum deadline. Maintaining states’ ability to request additional information within the statutory deadline will ensure determinations are timely and defensible.
To ensure the balance of cooperative federalism and further the purposes of this proposed rule change, Utah encourages clarity, consistency, and preservation of states’ rights. First, Utah supports a scope for 401 Certification consistent with cooperative federalism, preserving state authority to impose conditions necessary to protect its water resources and promote the welfare of its citizens. Second, to ensure consistency, Utah advocates for predictable timelines and standardized baseline requirements for certification requests and decisions, while allowing states flexibility to determine those requirements and timeline extensions – when extensions are mutually agreeable and in the best interest of the applicant. Third, states should retain the ability to address unique local conditions and impose requirements that safeguard each state’s water quality interests within a uniform federal framework that promotes consistency and clarity. Utah supports Congress’s policy that states are primary regulators of their own water and sees the State’s broad authority over 401 Certification as a successful application of this policy. 
PLEASE REFER TO THE ATTACHED LETTER FOR THE COMPLETE COMMENTS. THANK YOU

rationales.evidence: The letter cites legal authorities and references Sackett v. EPA, the Clean Water Act, and Federal Register language, but it provides limited concrete data, examples, or detailed citations beyond general legal references.
rationales.impact: It plausibly explains that drought, population growth, and land ownership pressures make water regulation important in Utah, but the claimed impacts are described at a high level rather than with specific quantified effects.

rationales.structure_formatting: The letter is organized into distinct paragraphs with a professional tone and clear thematic progression. However, it is somewhat repetitive and includes a placeholder directing readers to an attached letter, which limits completeness.
rationales.overall: This is a solid, relevant public comment that clearly advocates for state authority and procedural flexibility in section 401 certification. It is strongest on relevance and policy direction, but less strong on detailed evidence and specificity.

comment_text:
Comment on EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 - Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations.

I am writing on behalf of Minnesota Trout Unlimited and its thousands of members who fish the waters of the state to express strong opposition to the U.S. EPA's proposed rule revising the regulations implementing Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. Minnesota Trout Unlimited (MNTU) is familiar with Section 401 Certification process, since MNTU frequently undertakes stream habitat restoration projects around Minnesota. MNTU is required to obtain numerous state and federal permits and as well as 401 Certification from the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency. Although the 401 Certification process takes additional time and effort, the existing water quality certification process is important to prevent degradation of water quality and protect our cherished coldwater fisheries.
We oppose the changes to the rules proposed by EPA because they would substantially weaken long-standing state and Tribal authorities that are essential for protecting fish, wildlife, and the aquatic habitats they depend on. 
Section 401 is one of the Clean Water Act’s most important provisions for ensuring that federally permitted activities do not degrade water quality or impair designated uses, including the protection of fish and aquatic life. State and Tribal water quality certifications are essential opportunities to meaningfully address site-specific impacts to fish and wildlife from projects such as mines, pipelines, dredging, and other infrastructure projects. The changes to the rules EPA has proposed would significantly constrain that State and Tribal authority, putting Minnesota’s rivers, streams, and lakes at increased risk of pollution or damage.
Clean, healthy rivers, streams and lakes are crucial to support healthy fisheries, supply clean drinking water for downstream communities and to support numerous uses. Using the Section 401 certification process to evaluate the potential impacts of projects and development, and considering what additional conditions are warranted, is key to ensuring our state waters are not polluted or destroyed. 
We are particularly troubled by proposed rule’s narrowing of the scope of impacts that states and Tribes may consider as part of the Section 401 review process. Fish and wildlife are affected not just by direct discharges, but also by changes to flow regimes, habitat connectivity, temperature, and sediment transport. Many aquatic and riparian species, including migratory fish, amphibians, and waterfowl, are sensitive to these cumulative and secondary effects. Limiting review to discharge only, rather than the project as a whole, does not reflect ecological realities and undermines protection of biological integrity.
The proposed rule would also weaken State and tribal authority to require conditions necessary to avoid harm to fish and wildlife, such as seasonal construction restrictions to protect spawning or migration, minimum flow requirements to sustain aquatic habitat, and fish passage and screening. These types of state or tribal added conditions are often critical to prevent irreversible damage, including in waters already impacted by altered hydrology and habitat fragmentation.
Clean water is essential to healthy communities and economies. Continuing to allow States to protect State waterways through the 401 Certification process is far less expensive than taxpayers paying to restore or repair damaged ecosystems. is much more expensive than protecting them in the first place. Clean water and healthy fisheries produce healthy communities and economies. States and Tribes understand this. The EPA should not impede their efforts to protect our nations waters. The proposed rule would do just that - impede the thoughtful work of State and Tribal governments to protect our public waters and the fisheries they support.
MNTU urges the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing Section 401 procedures that allow States and Tribes to protect water quality, aquatic habitat, fisheries, and communities that rely on them. Our thousands of members are users of these important resources and demand the EPA do more to strengthen the Clean Water Act, rather than weaken it as the proposed rule would do. 
Sincerely,
John P. Lenczewski
Executive Director
Minnesota Trout Unlimited

rationales.relevance: The comment directly addresses EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 and focuses on Section 401 water quality certification, state/tribal authority, and the scope of review—core issues in the proposed rule.
rationales.reasoning: The argument is generally coherent and logically organized: it explains why the existing process matters, identifies specific concerns with narrowing review scope, and connects those concerns to ecological protection. Some claims are broad and repetitive, but the overall logic is clear.
rationales.evidence: The comment relies mostly on general assertions and organizational perspective rather than concrete data, citations, or specific examples from Minnesota projects or the rule text. It includes a few illustrative examples (mines, pipelines, seasonal restrictions) but little empirical support.
rationales.impact: The comment describes plausible harms such as pollution, habitat fragmentation, and reduced protection for fisheries, but the impacts are stated in broad terms without quantification or detailed case-specific consequences.
rationales.actionability: It gives a clear request to withdraw the proposed rule and retain existing Section 401 procedures. The recommendation is feasible and specific, though it does not propose alternative regulatory language or narrower revisions.
rationales.structure_formatting: The letter is readable and professionally framed, with a clear opening, body, and closing. There are minor grammatical issues and some repetition, but the overall organization is solid.
rationales.overall: This is a relevant and persuasive advocacy comment that clearly opposes the proposal and explains why. Its main weakness is the lack of supporting evidence and detailed, rule-specific analysis, but it is still a strong public comment letter.

overall_summary: A well-focused opposition comment that clearly targets the proposed Section 401 changes and offers a concrete ask to withdraw the rule. It is strongest on relevance and clarity, but would be more compelling with more specific evidence, citations, or examples.

comment_text:
The Massachusetts Rivers Alliance and the additional 12 organizations signed onto the the attached full comment letter are concerned that EPA’s proposed changes to the Section 401 certification process will reduce the quality of our waters by undermining the role of certifying agencies. We are particularly opposed to EPA’s proposal to limit the scope of 401 certification to impacts from discharges from point sources to navigable waters as contrary to both the text and purpose of the Clean Water Act. We urge EPA to not adopt the proposed changes.

The points are explained in further detailed in the attached letter:

I. We Oppose EPA’s Proposal to Narrow the Scope of 401 Certifications to Discharges from a Point Source to Navigable Waters.

A. Narrowing the scope of 401 certifications would contradict the plain language of Section 401.

B. Certifying authorities must be able to consider impacts to waterbodies protected under state law but that are not WOTUS.

C. Certifying authorities should be able to consider impacts from nonpoint source pollution.

D. Certifying authorities should be able to consider impacts to non-navigable waters.

II. EPA’s Proposal Would Undermine the Purpose of Section 401 and Certifying Authorities’ Ability to Protect Water Resources.

III. EPA’s Proposal Could Weaken Compliance with Public Notice Requirements.

IV. We Oppose EPA’s Proposal to Stop Treating Tribes as States for the Purpose of 401 Certification.

V. EPA Should Continue to Allow Modifications to the Grant of Certification Without the Agreement of the Applicant.

rationales.impact: It identifies plausible harms, such as reduced water quality protection and weakened certifying authority, but the impacts are stated generally rather than quantified or supported with specific examples.
rationales.actionability: The comment gives clear requests: do not adopt the proposed changes, retain broader certification scope, preserve Tribal treatment as States, and allow certification modifications without applicant agreement.
rationales.structure_formatting: The submission is well organized with a concise introduction and numbered sections/subsections that map to distinct issues, making it readable and professional.
rationales.overall: This is a strong, highly relevant advocacy comment with clear policy objections and actionable asks, but the excerpt lacks supporting evidence and detailed substantiation.

display_name: Clean Water for All et al.
comment_text:
The Clean Water for All Coalition and these 113 organizations strongly oppose the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed rule to again improperly weaken regulations related to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. Section 401 represents an important tool used by states and Tribes to protect state and Tribal water resources from the impacts of federally permitted development. Section 401 is a linchpin of the cooperative federalism structure envisioned by Congress when it passed the Clean Water Act in 1972 and is specifically designed to empower states and Tribes. The proposed rule would dramatically undercut the role provided to states and Tribes by the Act in protecting their waters.

The proposed rule will lead to more water pollution, more destruction of critical aquatic resources, more risk of flooding and other disasters, more threats to drinking water and public health, the loss of habitat, deprivation of recreational and other opportunities, and other negative consequences for our waters and the people – which is all of us – that rely on them.

We strongly urge you not to move forward with this ill-conceived and unnecessary rule and keep the existing 2023 rule in place.

rationales.relevance: The comment directly addresses EPA's proposed changes to Clean Water Act Section 401 certification and clearly states opposition to weakening state and Tribal authority, which is central to the docket.
rationales.reasoning: The argument is coherent at a high level: it asserts that Section 401 protects water resources and that weakening it would reduce protections. However, it remains largely conclusory and does not engage specific provisions of the proposed rule.
rationales.evidence: The comment provides no citations, data, examples, or specific factual support beyond broad assertions about harms and the role of Section 401.
rationales.impact: It identifies several potential harms, such as pollution, habitat loss, flooding risk, and drinking water threats, but these impacts are stated generally and without explanation of how the rule would plausibly cause them.
rationales.actionability: The request is clear in broad terms: do not finalize the rule and keep the 2023 rule in place. However, it does not offer more detailed, feasible alternatives or targeted revisions.
rationales.structure_formatting: The comment is concise and readable, with a clear opening, body, and closing request. It is professionally written, though not especially structured or detailed.
rationales.overall: This is a relevant and clearly opposed comment, but it is mostly advocacy language rather than a substantive regulatory critique. Its main weakness is the lack of evidence and specific engagement with the proposed rule's provisions.

overall_summary: The comment is highly relevant and clearly communicates opposition to the proposed Section 401 rule, but it is brief, largely unsupported by evidence, and offers only a general request to retain the current rule. It is readable and direct, but not especially persuasive as a detailed policy submission.

On behalf of Gunpowder RIVERKEEPER, I urge the EPA to withdraw its proposed revisions to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act that would limit the ability of states and Tribal governments to protect water quality.

Respectfully submitted,
 
Theaux M. Le Gardeur 
/S/ Theaux M. Le Gardeur

1207 Sparks Road

comment_text:
I am reaching out to express my staunch opposition to this proposed rule. While it would streamline and expedite permitting for major energy projects, it would also narrow the scope of Section 401 of the Clean Water Act, limiting state and tribal governments’ ability to protect waterways within their borders.

Section 401 has historically given state and tribal governments the authority to challenge large energy projects with long-term impacts on water quality, like oil and gas pipelines. But under the new rule, states and tribes would only be able to consider the immediate water quality impacts of a project when choosing to approve or reject it. They will essentially lose their ability to protect local waterways—even those that support their fisheries and drinking water supplies.

Consider a project like a dam. Even though the water released from it would pass water quality standards, the dam still impacts water flow and fish migration, both of which can have devastating impacts on river ecosystems and local communities in the long term.

As it stands, Section 401 has been instrumental in protecting water quality, and has rarely been “misused” to kill unwanted projects. Rather than gutting it to support fossil fuel projects and strip states and tribes of their ability to challenge them, we should be exploring ways to scale up wind, solar, and battery storage—energy sources that can provide power quickly, reliably, and affordably without jeopardizing the health of our waterways and the communities that rely on them.

Please do not finalize this harmful rule.

comment_text:
I am writing to express strong opposition to the U.S. EPA's proposed rule revising the regulations implementing Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. The proposed changes would substantially weaken long-standing state and Tribal authorities that are essential for protecting fish, wildlife, and the aquatic habitats upon which they depend. 

Section 401 has long served as one of the Clean Water Act’s most important tools for ensuring that federally permitted activities do not degrade water quality or impair designated uses, including the protection of fish and aquatic life. State and Tribal water quality certifications are an essential and sometimes the only meaningful opportunity to address site-specific impacts to fish and wildlife from projects such as dams, pipelines, transmission lines, dredging, and other infrastructure. The proposed rule would significantly constrain that authority, putting rivers and streams at increased risk of pollution or damage.

Healthy rivers and streams are important to support healthy fisheries, supply clean drinking water for downstream communities and to support a multitude of uses including irrigation and municipal use. It is essential that development with impact to these waters be properly evaluated and that any necessary conditions are put in place to ensure our waters are not polluted or destroyed. 

Of particular concern is the proposal’s narrowing of the scope of impacts that states and Tribes may consider as part of the 401-review process. Fish and wildlife are affected not only by the direct discharge, but also by other project impacts to waters including changes to flow regimes, habitat connectivity, temperature and sediment transport. Many aquatic and semi-aquatic species - including migratory fish, amphibians, freshwater mussels, and waterfowl – are highly sensitive to these cumulative and secondary effects. Limiting review to focus only on the discharge rather than the project as a whole fails to reflect ecological realities and undermines effective protection of biological integrity.

The proposed rule would weaken State and tribal authority to require the necessary conditions to mitigate or avoid harm to fish and wildlife, such as seasonal construction restrictions to protect spawning or migration, minimum flow requirements to sustain aquatic habitat, fish passage and screening, just to name a few. These conditions are often critical to preventing irreversible damage, particularly in waters already stressed by climate change, altered hydrology, and habitat fragmentation.

This proposed rule is especially concerning given the recent related proposal from the EPA and Army Corps to exclude all ephemeral streams, the majority of wetlands and an unknown number of intermittent stream miles from the regulatory protections of the Clean Water Act. Clean water is essential to healthy communities and economies. Restoring or repairing damaged ecosystems is much more expensive than protecting them in the first place. We should be working to increase protections for our nations waters, not weaken them.

I urge the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing procedures that allow states and Tribes to protect water quality, aquatic habitat, and the fish, wildlife and communities that rely on them. Any revisions to the Section 401 regulations should strengthen, not undermine, the Clean Water Act’s core objective: to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the nation’s waters.

Thank you for considering my views.

comment_text:
I am submitting this comment as a business leader in response to EPA's proposed update to the Water Quality Certification Regulations under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act.

My name is Roslyn Ogburn, and I am with GodsNaturalwonder@gmail.com, a business operating in Michigan. Like many businesses, ours depends on clean, reliable water to operate, manage costs, and plan for long-term investment.

Section 401 supports business certainty by ensuring that federally permitted projects account for water quality impacts early in the permitting process, when risks can be addressed at lower cost and with greater predictability. States and Tribes play a critical role in this process by applying locally appropriate standards, data, and technical expertise that reflect site-specific conditions and watershed characteristics. Preserving state rights and Tribal sovereignty is essential: the ability of local authorities to evaluate and condition projects ensures that water quality protections reflect local conditions, practical expertise, and the needs of communities and businesses that depend on clean water. Limiting this authority is a clear infringement on local control.

I am concerned that the proposed rule would narrow the range of impacts subject to review and limit the ability of states and Tribes to conduct meaningful, science-based evaluations grounded in local conditions. Excluding foreseeable impacts from review does not eliminate risk; it defers it. Those deferred risks often resurface later as project delays, operational constraints, costly retrofits, or litigation that is far more disruptive and expensive than early corrective action.

From a business perspective, predictability comes from identifying material risks early—not from discovering problems after financing, contracts, and construction timelines are already set. As proposed, the rule would reduce opportunities for early problem-solving and increase uncertainty for both businesses and public agencies.

I support reasonable streamlining that improves administrative clarity and reduces unnecessary duplication. However, efficiency should not come at the expense of substantive review. Limiting the ability to consider local water quality impacts simply shifts costs downstream and increases the overall economic burden.
I respectfully urge EPA to finalize a rule that preserves the authority of states and Tribes to assess and condition federally permitted projects based on local standards and foreseeable water quality impacts, while maintaining flexibility where additional technical review or consultation is warranted.

Clean water is a foundational economic asset. Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

comment_text:
Dear Administrator Zeldin,

I am concerned by the EPA proposal to weaken Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (CWA) and strongly oppose the proposed changes. 

The Clean Water Act provides states and authorized Tribes with an important tool to help protect water quality. The current proposed changes to Section 401 limit that scope in a detrimental manner that ties the hands of regulators and keeps them from looking beyond the pollution discharged into waterways to holistically evaluate the impact of a project on water quality. States and authorized Tribes need the ability to determine the scope of review that will protect water quality, not be limited to an ever narrowing scope of federally protected water and solely tasked to review direct water quality impacts of discharge into those waters. The broader water-quality effects caused by a project as a whole are what communities rely on the Clean Water Act to analyze and mitigate.

Water pollution has serious impacts, and any decision that threatens to increase pollution, harm public health, or exacerbate impacts to habitat needs to be analyzed and weighed. Waterways are not solely impacted in the spot where discharge occurs and limiting the scope of the Section 401 analysis would result in a lack of review of project impacts upstream and downstream. With the changes proposed, states and Tribes could lose the ability to use Section 401 to protect many smaller streams, wetlands and headwaters within their borders. This would render state and tribal decision makers powerless to block, or place conditions on, federally permitted projects that could damage those waters, even if they are vital to local drinking water supplies, fisheries, recreation, or flood control.

Limiting the scope and timeline for analysis to take place fails to achieve
the CWA goal of ensuring states, territories, and tribes are empowered to protect their water resources and instead only benefits the companies behind the proposed projects. It leaves taxpayers on the hook for additional cleanup of pollution that was unable to be mitigated because it was not analyzed under a discharge only scenario. It opens the door for projects that should not be permitted due to impacts and risks that would become clear during analysis, but are never properly reviewed. 

I call on the EPA to use its authority to uphold and strengthen the Clean Water Act to protect drinking water, public health, and species habitat in waterways and wetlands.

The Clean Water Act has been instrumental in protecting our country’s water sources for the past 50 years. Section 401 gives states, tribes, and local communities a seat at the table for determining the conditions of federal infrastructure projects–such as pipelines and dams. Rolling back section 401 is an attack on the ability of state and local authorities to place conditions on or even block these projects. Gutting this crucial part of the Clean Water Act is short sighted, and leaves state regulators powerless.

Protecting our clean water sources and increasing our energy capacity are not mutually exclusive. We can move forward with necessary energy projects without sacrificing our water sources to proven degradation and pollution. 

Please abandon the proposal to roll back section 401 of the Clean Water Act.

Sincerely,
Edward Reichman

comment_text:
I am writing in opposition to the Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 401 Water Quality Certification regulation. Section 401 is a cornerstone of the Clean Water Act’s cooperative federalism framework, providing states and authorized Tribes with the authority to ensure that federally permitted activities comply with water quality standards before pollution occurs. This preventive function is essential to protecting drinking water sources, wetlands, fisheries, and downstream communities from irreversible harm.¹
The proposed rule would significantly narrow how states and Tribes may exercise their Section 401 authority by restricting the scope of review, redefining what constitutes a complete certification request, and limiting the conditions that certifying authorities may impose.² While EPA characterizes these changes as procedural clarifications, their practical effect would be to constrain state and Tribal oversight and accelerate permitting timelines at the expense of water quality protection. This approach conflicts with the Clean Water Act’s express purpose “to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.”³
Section 401 has historically served as one of the most effective tools for protecting wetlands and headwater streams that are critical to downstream water quality, flood mitigation, and ecosystem function. Weakening this authority risks increasing reliance on post-hoc cleanup rather than prevention, shifting long-term environmental and financial burdens onto states, Tribes, and taxpayers. Environmental organizations and legal experts have warned that the proposed changes would reduce meaningful review of projects such as pipelines, hydropower facilities, and other infrastructure with well-documented risks to water resources.⁴
Of particular concern is how this proposal continues a broader pattern of undermining Tribal authority through regulatory action. Tribes are sovereign governments, not stakeholders, and many hold treaty-reserved rights to clean water, fisheries, and aquatic resources. Federal agencies have a legally enforceable trust responsibility to protect these rights. Any rule that limits the ability of Tribes to meaningfully review, condition, or deny certifications for projects affecting their waters or treaty resources undermines binding treaties and long-standing federal obligations.⁵
EPA has previously recognized that robust Tribal participation in water quality certification is essential to honoring Tribal sovereignty and protecting Tribal waters.⁶ Rolling back or narrowing this authority under the guise of efficiency erodes trust, weakens environmental justice protections, and disproportionately impacts Tribal nations and downstream communities that often bear the greatest consequences of water pollution.
For these reasons, EPA should withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule to preserve strong state and Tribal authority under Clean Water Act Section 401. Protecting clean water requires honoring the statute’s preventive intent, respecting Tribal sovereignty and treaty rights, and ensuring that economic development does not come at the cost of irreversible harm to waters and communities.
Footnote & Sources
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Clean Water Act Section 401 Certification
https://www.epa.gov/cwa-401
Federal Register, Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulation, Proposed Rule (January 15, 2026)
https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/15/2026-00754/updating-the-water-quality-certification-regulation
Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. §1251(a)
https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/33/1251
Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), EPA Proposal Would Curb States’ and Tribes’ Clean Water Act Oversight
https://www.nrdc.org/press-releases/epa-proposal-would-curb-states-and-tribes-clean-water-act-oversight

https://www.epa.gov/tribal/epa-policy-consultation-and-coordination-indian-tribes

https://www.epa.gov/wqs-tech/tribal-water-quality-standards

comment_text:
I am writing to express serious concern regarding proposed changes to Clean Water Act Section 401 that would weaken the authority of States and Tribes—particularly Tribes approved for “treatment as a State” (TAS) status—to review and certify federal permits and licenses for compliance with applicable water quality requirements.

Section 401 is a critical safeguard that ensures federally permitted activities do not undermine water quality standards established by States and Tribal Nations. For Tribes, this authority is not merely administrative; it is a core expression of Tribal sovereignty and self-determination, grounded in the federal trust responsibility and longstanding principles of environmental justice.

Any changes that limit, narrow, or preempt Tribal review authority risk disproportionately harming Tribal waters, treaty-protected resources, and culturally significant uses of water. Tribal Nations are best positioned to understand the ecological, cultural, subsistence, and spiritual importance of their waters, and their authority under Section 401 must be preserved—if not strengthened.

I strongly urge that any revisions to Section 401:

Fully preserve and respect Tribal sovereignty and TAS authority;

Avoid creating procedural or substantive barriers that undermine meaningful Tribal participation;

Ensure that Tribal water quality standards are given equal weight and enforceability as State standards; and

Enhance, rather than diminish, protections for waters of the United States, particularly those relied upon by Tribal communities.

Weakening Section 401 review authority would represent a step backward for clean water protections and for the federal government’s commitments to Tribal Nations. I respectfully request that these proposed changes be reconsidered to ensure that Tribal rights, authority, and water quality protections are preserved and enhanced.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

The benefit of greater efficiency by narrowing the regulation as proposed will only come with increased risks and a severe loss of protection. 

Under this proposed changed, states and tribal governments will lose their ability to protect local waterways—even those that support their fisheries and drinking water supplies.

It seems clear that the United States falling behind the rest of the world, rather than leading it in developing ways to scale up clean energy sources that can provide power quickly, reliably, and affordably without jeopardizing the health of our waterways and the communities that rely on them.

Please do not finalize this harmful rule.

comment_text:
I strongly oppose the EPA announced proposed revisions to the existing Section 401 water quality certification regulations. The definition of “water” will not take into account waterways such as city canals, and seasonal streams (or climate impacted) that flow under the surface and resurface to later join larger bodies of contiguous flow. It especially does not protect vulnerable wetlands and ponds with more complex dependencies. Areas that are currently impacted by climate and drought periods are not protected in the new language. Lastly I am particularly against the language that limits state/tribal authority to comment and challenge. Narrowing the scope of Section 401 violates the cooperative federalism structure of the CWA, which gives states and tribes primary responsibility to protect their own water quality.
Stop this assault now! It only benefits developers, miners, and oil interests at the loss to people of America that rely on clean, non-polluted water to survive under already stressed water conditions that are only increasing due to the administration’s refusal to accept the scientifically proved reality of human caused climate change. Meaning… the indirect and cumulative effects of polluting contributors that ultimately impact the habitat, culture, proven biologically imperatives, and health of our people and land must be considered. Not the small, short term impact, but rather the long term. Water discharge is not the sole contributor to water pollution!! Clean water is only possible with an understanding of the many factors that allow for healthy, non interrupted flow and filtering, and benefit the biology of a given area Projects that impede wetland health and habitat are only one example. Canals necessary for flushing in times of floods, watersheds sensitive to road construction which can wipe out the critical benefits of these watersheds for fire, fisheries, and flood control are additional examples of broader protection requirements. It’s not point-to-point discharge that must be reviewed, but the whole of water system and land impact. Only local states, tribes, and authorities have vested interest in protecting its people from direct and indirect water pollution and biological infringement! Only states and tribes have the knowledge that will be bypassed to fast track profit over people’s and lands health. This change in certification standards is unacceptable.

comment_text:
To Whom It May Concern,

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the EPA’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certification regulations (Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2025–2929).

I support efforts to make federal permitting more efficient and predictable. At the same time, I am concerned that aspects of the proposed rule risk narrowing Section 401 review in ways that could unintentionally weaken protections for wetlands—systems essential to water quality, flood control, and local economies.

I spend considerable time in both the Great Lakes region and South Florida. In both places, wetlands are not abstract features; they are central to how water moves, how nutrients are filtered, and how communities are protected from flooding and storms. These benefits are often indirect and cumulative, yet they are precisely how water quality is protected or degraded.

Wetlands reduce nutrient and sediment loading before water reaches rivers, lakes, and drinking-water supplies. When wetlands are lost or impaired, communities face higher treatment costs, increased harmful algal blooms, and declining fisheries. These impacts may appear local at first but accumulate across interconnected systems.

Wetlands also function as natural infrastructure. They store water, slow peak flows, and reduce downstream flooding during heavy rainfall and hurricanes. As extreme weather becomes more common, weakening safeguards that prevent wetland loss will likely increase long-term costs for disaster response, insurance, and infrastructure repair—far exceeding the short-term savings of faster permitting.

I also believe it is important to preserve the role Congress intended for states and tribes under Section 401. Local authorities understand their hydrology and watersheds in ways national rules cannot fully capture. Narrowing certification scope risks shifting long-term environmental and economic costs onto states while limiting their ability to prevent harm.

In this context, the Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett v. EPA should not be overextended. While the Court narrowed federal jurisdiction, it did not conclude that wetlands lacking a continuous surface connection are unimportant to water quality, nor did it disturb Congress’s broader purpose to protect the Nation’s waters. Section 401 remains a mechanism through which states may address water-quality impacts from intermittent, seasonal, or indirectly connected wetlands consistent with local hydrology.

EPA can streamline permitting without sacrificing wetland protection. I respectfully suggest:

1-Allow expedited or tiered review for projects with clearly minimal impacts, while preserving full Section 401 review where cumulative or downstream effects may occur.

2-Retain consideration of hydrologic connectivity, including seasonal surface and shallow subsurface flow, with clear standards.

3-Permit certification timelines to pause when applications are incomplete to avoid rushed decisions driven by procedural deadlines.

4-Encourage programmatic or watershed-scale certifications in sensitive regions.

5-Recognize wetlands as natural infrastructure that protects water quality and reduces flood risk.

6-Preserve state and tribal flexibility to tailor implementation to regional wetland systems.

In the Great Lakes, tributary wetlands retain phosphorus before it reaches nearshore waters; incremental losses contribute to basin-wide nutrient loading and harmful algal blooms, particularly in western Lake Erie. In South Florida, the Everglades depends on slow, shallow sheet flow; modest changes to wetland elevation or connectivity can disrupt flows, increase nutrients, and undermine decades of restoration investment. In both regions, hydrologic connectivity is foundational.

For these reasons, I urge EPA to revise the proposed rule to improve permitting efficiency through targeted procedural improvements while preserving the ability of certifying authorities to fully evaluate and protect wetlands and connected waters.

Thank you for considering these comments.

Sincerely,
John Weber

I am expressing strong opposition to the U.S. EPA's proposed rule revising the regulations implementing Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. The changes would substantially weaken long-standing state and Tribal authorities that are essential for protecting fish, wildlife, and the aquatic habitats upon which they depend. 

Healthy rivers and streams are important to support healthy fisheries, supply clean drinking water for downstream communities and to support a multitude of uses including irrigation and municipal use. It is essential that development with impact to these waters be properly evaluated and that any necessary conditions are put in place to ensure our waters are not polluted or destroyed. 

I urge the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing procedures that allow states and Tribes to protect water quality, aquatic habitat, and the fish, wildlife and communities that rely on them. Any revisions to the Section 401 regulations should strengthen, not undermine, the Clean Water Act’s core objective: to restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the nation’s waters.

Thank you,

I am deeply concerned about your agency’s proposed rule that eliminates Clean Water Act protections for many U.S. wetlands and streams. Protecting these water sources is deeply vital to our country's health and economic welfare.

America’s waterways are so interconnected that even weakening federal protections for wetlands anywhere will have a deep impact on clean water across the country. Wetlands are what protect us from extreme flood risk, keep our water flowing throughout the seasons, and replenish our floodplains so that we may continue to farm and ranch in Colorado. 

The proposal would increase flood risks, harm wildlife habitat, and threaten drinking water sources for millions of Americans. The EPA needs to protect our water sources, follow the best available science, and look out for all water users, not just oil and gas. The Proposed Rule would severely reduce the “waters of the United States” subject to protection under the Clean Water Act (CWA), 33 U.S.C. § 1251 et seq., without legal or scientific support. The Proposed Rule applies novel interpretations to narrow the meaning of “tributaries” and “wetlands” that qualify as “waters of the United States” and exclude altogether “interstate waters,” “prior converted cropland,” and “ditches” in ways that conflict with Congress’s intent, the agency’s longstanding interpretation, and judicial precedent. 

Additionally, Section 401 of the Clean Water Act allows tribes that can demonstrate the capacity and resources the ability to review water quality standards, expanding regulatory powers beyond tribes with larger resources. The proposed change would shrink those powers, allowing only TAS tribes to perform evaluations through a separate, more rigorous authorization program. This change would drastically reduce tribes' powers to protect their land and act on their treaty rights.

I stand with thousands of people across the nation who are united in opposition to any attempts to gut clean water protections. Please keep our critical waters protected and do not finalize this new rule.
