comment_text:
Date: 01/30/2026
To: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
Attention: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 
RE: Comments on Proposed Rule: Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations (CWA Section 401)

To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing as a concerned citizen Florida/Flagler County to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 401 Water Quality Certification regulations. Specifically, I am deeply concerned by the proposal to narrow the "scope of certification" from “activity as a whole" to a "discharge-only" focus. This change significantly undermines the ability of States and Tribes to protect local waters from the cumulative environmental impacts of large-scale projects.
1. Loss of Oversight for Cumulative Effects By limiting the scope of review to the specific point of discharge, the proposed rule ignores the broader reality of how large infrastructure projects—such as pipelines and dams—impact our ecosystems. Water quality does not exist in a vacuum; it is influenced by upland construction, clearing of riparian vegetation, and changes in local hydrology. Narrowing the review prevents states from assessing the cumulative effects of a project’s entire lifecycle, leaving our communities vulnerable to "death by a thousand cuts" where each individual discharge point may seem minor, but the project’s total impact is devastating.
2. Threats to Local Streams and Wetlands The proposed rule creates a dangerous gap in the protection of our most vulnerable water bodies. Wetlands and small headwater streams are the biological "kidneys" of our watersheds. Under the proposed "discharge-only" scope, a state may be forced to certify a project even if the construction of the project itself results in the destruction of non-jurisdictional wetlands or the degradation of streams through non-point source runoff.
• Specifically, to Flagler County we have the Matanzas River Basin and local wetlands. It is one of the last relatively undisturbed estuaries of Florida’s east coast, with nearly 35% of the basin comprised of critical wetlands. 
• Cumulative Development Pressure: With major land development projects currently sited in the headwaters of Pellicer, Moultrie, and Moses creeks, our watershed is already facing a projected increase in developed land use to over 25%. Under the proposed rule, the state would be unable to look at the: "activity as a whole" for these massive developments. This means they could be forced to ignore the cumulative loss of wetlands that act as our primary defense against storm surge and flooding—an issue that already causes "Moderate Flooding" levels (over 2.3 ft) at locations like Bings Landing.
• Wastewater and Infrastructure Strain: Palm Coast is currently grappling with wastewater capacity challenges, specifically at Wastewater Treatment Plant 1, which is nearing its permitted limits. By narrowing the scope of Section 401, the EPA would limit the ability of state regulators to ensure that new federal permits for large-scale projects do not exacerbate our existing infrastructure strain or lead to increased nutrient loading (nitrogen and phosphorus) that fuels harmful algal blooms in our canals and the Intracoastal Waterway.
• Pollution and Runoff: My community already faces threats from stormwater runoff carrying pesticides, sediments, and bacteria into our waterways. The proposed rule would prevent the state from placing necessary conditions on a project’s construction phase (like upland erosion control) simply because those impacts aren't tied to a specific "point source" pipe. This will inevitably lead to more pollution in our local streams and the degradation of the delicate salt marshes that protect our coastline.

3. Erosion of Cooperative Federalism Section 401 was designed by Congress to ensure that federal licenses do not bypass state water quality standards. This proposal shifts the balance of power away from the local experts and communities who best understand their own watersheds and hands it back to federal agencies that may prioritize project speed over local environmental health.
Conclusion I urge the EPA to maintain the 2023 Rule's "activity as a whole" scope. Protecting our water requires a holistic approach that considers how a project actually functions in the real world, not just how it looks at the end of a single pipe. I ask the Agency to prioritize the health of our local streams, wetlands, and families over regulatory shortcuts for industry.
Sincerely,
Brittany Myers

comment_text:
I am writing to you as a Coloradan who cares deeply about the health of our mountain streams and the future of my family's outdoor traditions. I am reaching out to express my strong opposition to the EPA's proposed changes to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. These changes would strip away the power of our state and local Tribes to protect the very water that sustains our communities, our farms, and our world-class fisheries.

In Colorado, our rivers are our lifeblood. Section 401 has historically been one of our most effective tools for ensuring that large projects like dams, pipelines, and transmission lines do not ruin the water quality we rely on. For decades, it has given our state the right to review these projects and set common-sense conditions to protect fish and wildlife. By weakening this authority, the federal government is effectively telling us that we no longer have a say in protecting our own backyard from the impacts of industrial development.

This proposal is particularly concerning because it narrows the focus to only "direct discharge" of pollution, ignoring the bigger picture of how a project actually affects a river. As someone who spends time on the water, I know that fish aren't just affected by what is dumped into a stream. They are affected by changes in water temperature, flow levels, and the loss of habitat connectivity. If a project dries up a stream bed or blocks a spawning run, the damage is just as real as if a chemical was spilled. We need to be able to consider the whole project, not just a small part of it.

For my family, this isn't just a policy debate. It is about whether or not our kids will still be able to find healthy trout in our mountain streams twenty years from now. If we lose the ability to require seasonal construction restrictions or minimum flow requirements, we risk losing the biological integrity of our waters forever. These safeguards are especially vital now, as our rivers are already stressed by drought and a changing climate.

Protecting our headwaters is a matter of fiscal and environmental responsibility. It is much cheaper to protect a stream today than it is to try to restore a ruined ecosystem tomorrow. This rule, combined with other recent efforts to remove protections for wetlands and smaller streams, represents a massive step backward for Colorado.

I urge you to stand up for our state's right to protect its own resources. Please ask the EPA to withdraw this rule and instead support policies that maintain the chemical, physical, and biological health of our nation's waters. Our rivers and the families who enjoy them deserve nothing less.

comment_text:
Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929 
I submit this comment in response to EPA’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act (CWA) §401 Water Quality Certification regulations. I am interested in this regulation because I work in environmental compliance, permitting, and regularly operate within multi‑agency regulatory frameworks. My experience includes navigating federal, state, and local environmental regulations and how they apply at my facility. I am generally supportive of the proposed rule’s objective of improving clarity and procedural consistency in the §401 certification process.
This comment focuses on the portions of the proposal that clarify the scope of §401 certification review, standardize application completeness expectations, and define procedural elements such as timelines and certification conditions tied to water quality impacts. These components are especially important in practice because they shape how certification requests are evaluated across jurisdictions, and this can be a recurring challenge in environmental permitting due to the variation in how §401 certification is implemented. 
Differences in how agencies define completeness, scope of review, and allowable certification conditions can create uncertainty, delay, and inconsistent expectations for project advocates. When procedural standards are unclear or highly variable, both regulators and applicants spend additional time resolving threshold issues rather than focusing on substantive water quality protections.
EPA’s proposal to standardize core procedural elements, including completeness criteria and review scope, would improve predictability and transparency while preserving the important role of states and tribes in protecting water quality. By focusing certification review on point‑source discharges into federally regulated waters and on water‑quality‑related impacts, the proposal provides clearer guidance on the intended scope of certification decisions. In complex permitting environments involving multiple agencies, clearer jurisdictional and subject‑matter boundaries improve coordination and reduce confusion.
From a rulemaking perspective, this proposal is not only a technical regulatory update but also an example of how agencies recalibrate the balance between uniform federal standards and state‑level discretion within a cooperative federalism framework.
The proposal identifies implementation inconsistency and procedural uncertainty as current challenges and responds with clearer procedural standards. More defined expectations around completeness, timelines, and certification conditions should support more consistent decisions and more transparent outcomes across jurisdictions. My participation here is offered to assist in improving the final rule. In presenting these comments, I aim to follow sound rulemaking advocacy practices, including reasoned analysis, attention to statutory structure, and respect for the agency’s procedural obligations.
For these reasons, I encourage EPA to adopt the proposed clarifications to scope and procedure in the final rule. I also recommend that the final rule maintain appropriate operational flexibility for state and tribal authorities to address site‑specific water quality conditions when supported by the administrative record.
Clear procedural standards, well‑defined review scope, and transparent decision criteria benefit agencies, regulated entities, and the public. They improve predictability while supporting effective environmental protection. I appreciate EPA’s effort to refine and clarify the §401 framework and respectfully submit these comments for consideration.

comment_text:
I oppose the EPA’s proposed revisions to the Clean Water Act Section 401 water quality certification regulations with respect to the scope of waters clause.

The notion that waters beyond the borders of the united states should not be considered ignores the situation of the Great Lakes, namely that one large body of water is shared with Canada. When a body of water is shared in this way, what affects one side affects both sides. A US entity such as Enbridge could choose to run a pipeline through Canadian waters in order to avoid US or State of Michigan or State of New York review. Yet any poor design or planning would still affect the US and those states since it is the same body of water and we cannot pretend an oil spill on the Canadian side will deign to only kill Canadian fish or spoil Canadian shoreline. 

Further, the idea of focusing on "navigable waters" ignores the fact that a navigable body of water might be linked to non-navigable bodies of water within a given ecosystem or drainage basin - but what happens to one body of water again will happen to them all. The existing rules account for this, the proposed changes do not.

Further, it is inappropriate to focus solely on "discharge from a point source". Again, with pipelines. There might be a single point source, there might not even be a "discharge" - at the time of construction. However, a pipeline can break, thus creating a point source discharge where there was not one. Thus the review needs to consider not only where a discharge currently exists, but also where one might occur as a result of the activity under review, which means a review of the entire system. 

There is a temptation to attempt to strictly focus on the pure text of what is in a law from Congress, however all regulations and rulings involve _some_ amount of interpretation. 

The motivation for these rule changes is stated to be to clarify, simplify, and to speed along regulatory approvals. These are laudable goals. However, there is also risk that these goals are pursued solely in the shorter-term economic interest of business, at the expense of the greater public good - notably, the longer-term goals of having clean water for everyone. Clean water is vital to life, much as clean air is, and sometimes it is necessary to impose economic costs on business in the short term to ensure the public good in the longer term.

comment_text:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the USEPA’s proposed rule issued on January 16 that would weaken Section 401 of the Clean Water Act and limit the ability of states and tribes to protect their waterways from pollution caused by federally permitted energy projects.

Section 401 has, for decades, served as a critical safeguard by allowing states and tribes to review and, when necessary, deny permits for projects that threaten local water quality. This provision reflects the reality that state and local governments are best positioned to understand the unique ecological, public health, and economic needs of their watersheds. Curtailing this authority undermines cooperative federalism and strips communities of a vital tool to protect their drinking water, wetlands, rivers, and streams.

The proposed rule would make it easier to construct oil and gas pipelines, coal export terminals, and other large-scale energy infrastructure projects while reducing meaningful oversight of their impacts on local waterways. This change would increase the risk of pollution, habitat destruction, and long-term damage to water resources that millions of people depend on for drinking water, recreation, and livelihoods.

The justification that this rule change is necessary to supply electricity to data centers is insufficient and troubling. Expanding energy infrastructure should not come at the expense of clean water protections or public health. Sustainable energy planning must prioritize environmental safeguards rather than weaken long-standing laws designed to prevent pollution before it occurs.

This proposal follows recent efforts to roll back federal protections for wetlands and streams, further eroding the Clean Water Act’s core purpose. Together, these actions represent a significant step backward in protecting the “waters of the United States,” contrary to the intent of Congress and the public interest.

I urge the USEPA to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the full authority of states and tribes under Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. Protecting clean water is not an obstacle to progress—it is a fundamental responsibility and a cornerstone of environmental justice, public health, and long-term economic stability.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

comment_text:
I am concerned that the proposed rule limits state and tribal authority, narrows the review of water quality impacts to an unrealistic scope, and prioritizes permitting speed over protecting water quality and public health. These changes risk overlooking cumulative pollution, local conditions, and downstream impacts that directly affect communities.
I oppose the proposed updates to the Water Quality Certification Regulations because they weaken important safeguards that protect water resources people rely on every day for drinking, fishing, farming, and recreation. By restricting what states and tribes are allowed to consider during certification, the proposal may fail to account for how pollution actually behaves in the environment, including runoff, sedimentation, and pollutants that accumulate over time or travel downstream.
From an environmental health perspective, water quality cannot be separated from human health. Even small increases in pollution can contribute to long-term health risks, especially for children, older adults, and communities already facing higher environmental burdens. Wetlands, headwaters, and smaller waterways play a critical role in filtering pollutants and protecting downstream water supplies, yet these areas are more likely to be overlooked under a narrower review process.
The proposal also places strict limits on timelines and standardizes information requirements in a way that may reduce meaningful review. While efficiency is important, rushing decisions or restricting the ability of certifying authorities to request additional information may lead to incomplete evaluations and missed risks. Local and tribal agencies are often best positioned to understand site-specific conditions, historical pollution concerns, and community health impacts, and their expertise should be preserved rather than constrained.
Additionally, limiting state and tribal authority undercuts the cooperative federalism framework that is central to the Clean Water Act. States and tribes have long served as a frontline defense in protecting water quality, and reducing their role could lead to weaker protections and increased public health risks over time.
While timely infrastructure development is important, it should not come at the expense of clean water, public health, or community trust. I urge EPA to reconsider these proposed changes and retain a more flexible, comprehensive approach that allows states and tribes to fully evaluate potential water quality and health impacts before certifications are granted.

Sincerely,
Zenon Kane, MD
Occupation and Environmental Medicine Resident Physician

comment_text:
I strongly oppose the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)’s proposed revisions to Clean Water Act Section 401 Water Quality Certifications. For well over 50 years, Section 401 of the Clean Water Act has been a critical tool to allow states and the federal government to cooperatively manage our shared water resources—and ensure that local voices are not disregarded in the process. This proposed rulemaking—which is being carried out under an order to make it easier for oil and gas infrastructure to be built, not to better safeguard our waters– is contrary to the language of the Clean Water Act and would greatly restrict states’ and Tribes’ long-standing authority to protect waters within their borders.

Water Quality Certification is one of the most important and effective tools available to states and Tribes to ensure federally-licensed projects are protective of water quality for drinking and recreation, and aquatic habitat for fish and wildlife. The proposed rule would greatly undermine state and Tribal authority to protect their waters by restricting the type of protective conditions states and Tribes can put on federally licensed or permitted activities that threaten state or Tribal waters. 

Additionally, the proposed rule would restrict the timeline and information for state and Tribal review. States and Tribes must have adequate time and information to review and process complex applications and the ability to impose conditions on permits that will protect water quality, especially given the differences in types of resources and water quality standards between states. 

In 2023, the EPA appropriately reasserted the strong role that states and Tribes should have in protecting their waters. This strong role - which has been the norm for most of the last 55 years - does not need to be weakened. I urge you to withdraw this damaging proposal immediately. I instead ask you to uphold the longstanding state and Tribal authority to protect waters within their boundaries.

comment_text:
On behalf of the National Wildlife Federation and affiliate partners from Missouri, along with our millions of members and supporters, we write in opposition to the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposal to again revise regulations related to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (CWA or the Act), a tool used by states and Tribes to protect state and Tribal water resources from the impacts of federally permitted or licensed projects. This proposed rule largely recycles an ill-conceived rule issued in 2020 that upended almost fifty years of strong state and Tribal authority to ensure that projects such as dams, pipelines, highways, and data centers are protective of state and Tribal waters and the important services they provide to both people and wildlife. The 2020 rule was subsequently replaced in 2023 by a rule that restored the strong proper role for states and Tribes envisioned by the Act while making some needed updates. We urge the EPA to keep the 2023 rule in place.
This proposal flies in the face of established science, and could potentially endanger our most precious natural resource, our drinking water.
The proposed rule is unnecessary and harmful while undermining state and Tribal sovereignty. It would violate the Act by rejecting its clear meaning and overturning Supreme Court precedent by limiting the scope of certification from the activity to the discharge from a point source of a project. This would dramatically limit the ability of states and Tribes to look at the totality of potential impacts and harms to waters from a project. For instance, it could eliminate or undermine state and Tribes from being able to put in place protective measures so that rivers and streams have adequate flow, habitat is protected, fish passage can occur, and that public access to designated uses like fishing and recreation is maintained.
It undercuts the ability of states to ensure they have the information they need to assess how various projects may impact their waters. It improperly gives the applicant an effective veto over modifications to protective conditions if a project changes. And it appears to remove the ability of states and Tribes to protect non-federal waters with 401 certification – a critical rollback given that EPA is considering a rule that would leave less than 20 percent of historically covered wetlands and only a fraction of historically covered headwater streams still federally jurisdictional. Finally, it limits the ability of states to protect other water quality-related requirements of state law by narrowing the definition of these requirements to applicable and appropriate state or water-quality related requirements for discharges only. This would make it harder for states to protect things like flow and habitat.
The 2023 rule adequately addressed any concerns regarding uncertainty around timing or process while clarifying that certification, conditions, and denial must regard water quality requirements. It did this while restoring the broad and longstanding ability of states and Tribes to protect their waters, as envisioned by the Act. This proposal amounts to little more than a needless weakening of that ability for no reason. The Section 401 process rarely results in the denial or undue delay of projects. For example, as EPA’s Economic Analysis shows, almost all permits issued by the Corps (which make up the overwhelming number of permits subject to Section 401) are either granted (95.5%) or waived (3.8%). Only 0.8% are denied.
Furthermore, consider recent significant changes to the scope of Clean Water Act protections generally. Section 401 is only triggered when a federal permit or license involving a discharge to waters of the United States is at issue. Most federal permits and licenses that trigger Section 401 are Section 404 discharge permits under the Clean Water Act itself. In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a decision in Sackett v. EPA that dramatically reduced the number of waters covered by the federal Clean Water Act. Adding to this, the EPA is now finalizing a rule that would even further limit the number of waters protected by the Act. comment_text:
I strongly oppose the proposed changes to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. For 50 years, this provision has provided essential protection for our nation's waterways by giving states and authorized tribes the ability to review federally permitted projects that could affect their water quality.

The proposed rule would significantly limit this authority by restricting reviews to only "direct discharges" into waterways, rather than allowing comprehensive assessments of broader environmental impacts. This change would weaken local communities' ability to protect drinking water sources, fisheries, wetlands, and cultural resources.

Furthermore, the proposed strict deadlines and limited review scope would accelerate project approvals without ensuring adequate environmental protection. This comes at a particularly concerning time, following recent judicial decisions that have already reduced federal water protections.

Water is a shared resource that sustains communities, ecosystems, and economies. Once contaminated, restoration can take generations. The current Section 401 authority provides essential safeguards that allow local communities to protect their water resources for current and future generations.

I urge the EPA to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the current authority that allows states and tribes to conduct meaningful water quality reviews. Our nation's waterways deserve comprehensive protection, not weakened standards that prioritize expedited project approvals over environmental stewardship.

comment_text:
***The Clean Water Act makes plain that states may veto Section 401 permits for infrastructure projects that cause gratuitous harm to aquatic ecosystems in that state, correctly reflected in the 1971 rule. The purpose of this clause is vividly demonstrated today. The authors of the Clean Water Act anticipated that one day, the EPA leadership offices would be occupied by scientifically and morally illiterate men, ambitious for power and favor, who say EPA's mission is to unleash American industry. They would purge EPA of its responsibility to protect our streams and wetlands from economic interests, and instead join industry in shuffling along this destruction, disdainful and oblivious to the destruction of biodiversity, hydrological systems, and human health. This has now come to pass. They anticipated that one day, vapid, hand-waving appeals to nebulous concepts like ‘vital infrastructure,' or ‘national interest,' or this Administration's fetish, ‘energy dominance,' could be wielded to discard Americans' love for the very things that make life worth living, and make America a worthwhile place to live. 

In my former home state of Oregon, the Department of Environmental Quality vetoed the so-called ‘Jordan Cove Liquified Natural Gas' Project in 2019 using its section 401 authority. This was a correct choice, and the people of Oregon and America are better off for it. EPA would define out of existence the capacity of Oregon to choose whether it wishes to be a sacrifice zone. This cautionary scenario is repeatable any time that a company with no care either for the people and life of a place, or for the future, draw a line on a map showing all to be bulldozed, erasing everything beautiful, precious, and valuable in the way. Section 401 is a tool for humans with values not measured in dollars or in barrels or cubic feet to assert their right to a quality of life, and to a healthy local ecosystem.

America has lost the majority of its wetlands already. The extinction crisis is especially pronounced in aquatic ecosystems. Simultaneously, extremes of flood and drought are magnified by climate change, whether this Administration believes it or not. Our remaining wetlands, aquifers, and tributary streams are more precious than ever in buffering these extremes. This Section 401 guardrail against combined, federal-corporate voracious power is more vital than ever. If EPA hands industry the tools to steamroll the love of Americans for our last aquatic ecosystems, the Trump Administration will leave our children with great ‘energy dominance,' but a bleak, barren, meaningless world stripped of natural life, and a traumatic, harried struggle for survival between droughts and floods.*** 

I am writing to urge EPA to withdraw its proposed revisions to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. I believe this proposal would drastically limit the ability of states and Tribal governments to protect water quality.

Federally permitted projects can threaten drinking water, fisheries, and public health if proper safeguards are not in place.

Section 401 embodies cooperative federalism and ensures that local expertise and community voices are not overridden by federal permitting decisions. Weakening this authority would disproportionately harm frontline and underserved communities and make it harder to prevent pollution before it occurs.

The proposed rule undermines decades of effective clean water protections and prioritizes industry convenience over the public interest. I urge EPA to reject this proposal and fully uphold Section 401 as Congress intended.

Thank you.

Hello,

This new rule will limit the ability of states to block the construction of oil, and gas pipelines, coal export terminals, and other energy projects that in all likely hood will pollute local waterways. This ruling will lessen the oversight of local officials and communities have on how their water supplies are protected. The local community should decide what we want, and how the community will best be served in the protection of our local resources, and not by lessening our protections. This rule will not make us healthier, or the local communities wealthier. Data Centers, for example, employ few people, use vast amounts of energy and water. Please do not weaken Section 401. We do not want it, or need it. The local communities should decide under the current guidelines, what best suits our needs. 
Thank you,
Monica Dechering

As someone who has worked on both sides of CWA regulations, I know that the rules and regulations can seem cumbersome but let's remember what brought about the Clean Water Act in the first place. Without rules and regulations our waters were full of offal and chemicals. So much so that in Missouri some residents recount the, " overpowering smells of blood, piss, and decaying flesh." In Cleveland, Ohio the Cuyahoga River was so full of flamable chemicals that it often caught fire. Obviously, we Americans are not capable of preserving the environment over our own profit. 

New definitions of Waters of the United States, as currently proposed, will lead to a decrease in regulated waters and thus to increased pollution. This increased pollution will directly effect downstream waters, which are regulated, and make them less fishable and swimmable, two standards of the Clean Water Act. This lowered water quality will also impact the health of all Americans who come into contact with it, whether physical contact or through treatment of the waters to make them potable. 
Proposal's to limit the 401 enforcement abilities of the states and tribes will also have a negative impact on those waters removed from requlation. Aside from the negative impacts to water quality, the following negative health impacts to citizens and the degradation of natural systems, it is also and affront to states rights. The Clean Water Act was written to allow states to enact rules and regulations more strict than federal laws.
There should be no degradation of the Clean Water Act if you care about the health of this countries natural resources or it's human population.

I hope the EPA will support our people, communities, and wildlife in Southern Oregon and withdraw its proposed revisions to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act that would limit states' and Tribal governments' ability to protect water quality.

Sincerely,

comment_text:
The Clean Water Act makes plain that states may veto Section 401 permits for infrastructure projects that cause gratuitous harm to aquatic ecosystems in that state, correctly reflected in the 1971 rule. The purpose of this clause is vividly demonstrated today. The authors of the Clean Water Act anticipated that one day, the EPA leadership offices would be occupied by scientifically and morally illiterate men, ambitious for power and favor, who say EPA’s mission is to unleash American industry. They would purge EPA of its responsibility to protect our streams and wetlands from economic interests, and instead join industry in shuffling along this destruction, disdainful and oblivious to the destruction of biodiversity, hydrological systems, and human health. This has now come to pass. They anticipated that one day, vapid, hand-waving appeals to nebulous concepts like ‘vital infrastructure,’ or ‘national interest,’ or this Administration’s fetish, ‘energy dominance,’ could be wielded to discard Americans’ love for the very things that make life worth living, and make America a worthwhile place to live. 

In my former home state of Oregon, the Department of Environmental Quality vetoed the so-called ‘Jordan Cove Liquified Natural Gas’ Project in 2019 using its section 401 authority. This was a correct choice, and the people of Oregon and America are better off for it. EPA would define out of existence the capacity of Oregon to choose whether it wishes to be a sacrifice zone. This cautionary scenario is repeatable any time that a company with no care either for the people and life of a place, or for the future, draw a line on a map showing all to be bulldozed, erasing everything beautiful, precious, and valuable in the way. Section 401 is a tool for humans with values not measured in dollars or in barrels or cubic feet to assert their right to a quality of life, and to a healthy local ecosystem.

America has lost the majority of its wetlands already. The extinction crisis is especially pronounced in aquatic ecosystems. Simultaneously, extremes of flood and drought are magnified by climate change, whether this Administration believes it or not. Our remaining wetlands, aquifers, and tributary streams are more precious than ever in buffering these extremes. This Section 401 guardrail against combined, federal-corporate voracious power is more vital than ever. If EPA hands industry the tools to steamroll the love of Americans for our last aquatic ecosystems, the Trump Administration will leave our children with great ‘energy dominance,’ but a bleak, barren, meaningless world stripped of natural life, and a traumatic, harried struggle for survival between droughts and floods.

comment_text:
Attn: Administrator Lee Zeldin, and Lauren Kasparek, Oceans, Wetlands and Communities Division, Office of Water
Re: Docket # EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929

Dear Sir and Madam:

My name is Emily, and I write as a concerned Michigan citizen. Living in the midst of a watershed to the world's largest source of fresh water, I am understandably concerned about planned changes to the Clean Water Act's certification registrations. I will refer to sections and pages of FRL-6976.2-01-OW from January 15 as needed. On that note, I second the statement from the Attorney Generals that this comment period should be extended for another month to grant a meaningful chance for comment. Below, I will list particular areas for concern.

First, the original definition involved "Activity" that could lead to polluting discharges (IV-B, par. 3, p. 2012). I worry that changing the definition to "discharge" alone (V-C-2, p. 2023-4, and V-C-2-v, p. 2026-7) might lead to allowing more harm, since much water pollution also comes from non-point sources such as urban runoff and rural fertilizers, and delayed point-source discharges that arise from processes, such as minerals eroded during construction.

I also worry about the narrowing of Waters of the U.S. to "navigable waters" alone, since many pollutants leach in via smaller streams, snowmelt, groundwater, and other sources from the land-based watershed.

Another concern is that amending the scope of who can address the application by changing "Neighboring Jurisdictional Leader/Regional Administrator" to simply "Administrator" (V-F, pp. 2031-2) would mean that any administrator could address this. I would prefer that regional administrators, who are close to the problem site and can more easily understand the situation, address regional problems, over those more remote with less vested interest in the site.

I understand the desire to streamline processes in the name of economic efficiency (VI-A, p. 2037), and belief that Executive Order 14192 is the easiest way to it (VII-B, P. 2038). However, the costs to local livelihoods and the long-term loss of materials for business might outweigh any short-term gains. While amending the act itself might not directly impact human health (VII-H, p. 2040), what these changes permit most assuredly could.

Many in our state and neighboring ones have a vested interest in protecting the Great Lakes and their adjoining ecosystems and communities. They tie into tourism, fishing, shipping, recreation, brewing, local traditions, and so much more. It is thus imperative that we leave the Clean Water Act as it is, even strengthen its effectiveness, so that we can continue to protect our waters for generations, and continue to thrive.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Dear Environmental Protection Agency: 

On behalf of myself and my family, I urge the EPA to reconsider its recent update of Section 401 of the Clean Water Act limiting the ability of states and tribal governments to review projects and possibly block them if they threaten waterways, wetlands, and ultimately, clean, drinking water. 

We live in a region which depends on clean, natural waterways and water bodies, i.e., rivers and streams, lakes, ocean and inland seawater bodies. We are blessed with an abundance of them, and our state tribal governments have protected them over many years--for tribes over centuries. Local and regional athorities are best situated to offer protection because they know these waters best and they depend daily on their health.

Federal and state cooperation is foundational to America's system of government, and Section 401 has been critical to putting the public's interest above the wants of polluters. After recent rollbacks of federal clean water protections, state, tribal and local input has become even more necessary.

The Spokane River, the Skagit River, and above all the Columbia have depended upon and benefited from the wise historic protection from tribal nations and more recently from Washington State oversight.

The EPA's proposed rule weakening Section 401 undermines the will of Americans who want clean water protections and the ability of states and tribes to review and possibly block projects that may threaten public health and degrade the waterways and wetlands within their borders. I urge the EPA to not adopt the proposed revisions to Section 401.

Sincerely,

comment_text:
Dear EPA,
I urge your to withdraw the proposed revisions to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act, which would limit the ability of states and Tribal governments to protect water quality for their people. My community depends on water quality protections in the Mad River and Eel River basins of northwest California to ensure that our drinking water is safe, to protect public health, and to protect the fisheries that the Mad River supports.

It is essential for the Clean Water Act to retain the ability of states and Tribes to review federally permitted projects within our watersheds. States rights to clean water should not be limited by federal CWA rules such as those currently proposed. Section 401 ensures that local expertise and community voices are not overridden by federal permitting decisions. Weakening this authority would harm our communities and the health of our watersheds, by making make it harder to prevent their pollution.

The proposed rule undermines the intent of the Clean Water Act, and threatens the decades of effective clean water protections it has provided us. Instead, the proposal prioritizes industry convenience over the public interest. I urge EPA to reject this proposal and fully uphold Section 401 as Congress intended.
Thank you.

comment_text:
The Clean Water Act is the nation’s most effective tool to protect the waterways in all our communities. Protecting states’ and tribes’ ability to curb projects that could jeopardize wetlands, rivers, and streams is a win for the health of our environment over the financial interests of corporate polluters. 
An important part of the Clean Water Act provides states and tribes the power to protect their waters from harmful pollution caused by federally approved projects.
State and Tribal authority under the Clean Water Act is based on the idea of federal and state cooperation, providing states the opportunity to prioritize their specific needs to protect their water.
The Trump administration’s rollback of state and tribal authority under the Clean Water Act is intended to fast track projects and save developers money while making it harder for states and tribes to limit water quality harms from these projects. This puts water quality at risk for millions of Americans.
Clean water protections should not be sacrificed for the benefit of polluting industries with deep pockets. All communities deserve safe, reliable water free from contamination.
This rule change proposes a solution for a problem that does not exist. The proposed change is nothing more than giving industries an easier path to pollute. The Trump administration has provided no reasonable justification for its proposed rule, only stating that it is preferred by industrial interests.
Defending state and tribal authority under the Clean Water Act is essential to providing states and tribes a say in protecting water quality, promoting public health, and ensuring environmental justice for all.

Re: Docket ID EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929
I am a resident of Bethel, Vermont and I recreate on public lands and waters with my family. Please do not weaken the ability of states and authorized Tribes to protect water quality through Clean Water Act Section 401 certification.

Clean water is the foundation for public health, fish, wildlife, and the outdoor economy that depends on public access. In my experience on the White and Tweed Rivers here in Vermont, enforceable water quality standards and enforceable certification conditions help determine whether habitat stays fishable, swimable and whether downstream communities can rely on safe water. My region’s local economy benefits from the people who come to fish and recreate on these rivers. 

I urge you to preserve meaningful state and Tribal authority to apply water quality requirements and attach enforceable conditions that protect watersheds and downstream communities.

Thank you for considering my comments.

comment_text:
Dear Administrator Zeldin, 

I’m writing as a concerned citizen to communicate my opposition to the Environmental Protection Agency's proposed changes to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. This proposed rule would limit both state and Tribal governments ability to limit projects that threaten our valuable water resources– waterways, wetlands, and drinking water. 

The proposed rule seeks to undermine environmental protection and limit the rights of states and Tribes to protect their water resources. The current procedures set in the 2023 Rule allow for flexibility for state and Tribal governments to assess risks to their communities. The 2023 Rule certification process serves to prevent irreversible, costly damage to our waterways. This process would be reversed if the proposed rule is not amended. 

The Clean Water Act is so important because it seeks to protect one of the most valuable resources in our country. Water’s ability to flow and move underground, while vital for our survival, complicates regulation and protection. Someone or something will always be downstream of other’s actions. This proposed rule, while seeking to shorten and streamline the certification process for projects, decreases the ability to consider environmental and human health impacts on these proposed projects. Protecting our nation’s water resources should not be rushed.

Additionally, I am respectfully requesting that the comment period be extended beyond the current 30-day comment period. The monumentally important Clean Water Act and its proposed rules should be considered significant rulemaking and the public comment period should be at a minimum 60 days if not longer. As was stated in Section A of this Federal Register document, “the Agency welcomes comments on whether the proposed definition is necessary and addresses concerns”. 30 days is hardly sufficient time for all the interested parties to prepare and submit comments. 

I strongly urge EPA to not adopt the proposed rule changes to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. Thank you for the opportunity to share my comment and concerns for the citizens of this country.

Best, 
A Concerned Citizen

comment_text:
Public Comment Opposing Proposed Revisions to Clean Water Act Section 401 Regulations — Florida Waters
Docket: EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929

I oppose EPA’s January 13, 2026 proposal to revise the Clean Water Act Section 401 water quality certification regulations.

Florida demonstrates why Section 401 must remain strong. Our state sits on porous limestone karst geology where pollution travels rapidly through groundwater into springs, rivers, wetlands, estuaries, and drinking water aquifers. Contamination rarely stays at a discharge point — it moves through connected waters and affects communities far from the original source. Even small upstream discharges can degrade world-renowned Florida springs that depend on clean groundwater.

Section 401 allows states and Tribes to evaluate the full impacts of federally permitted projects and require conditions necessary to protect water quality. The proposed rule would improperly narrow that review to a limited discharge analysis and prevent consideration of broader and cumulative impacts. That approach ignores real-world hydrology and undermines the authority Congress intentionally preserved for states.

In Florida, upstream decisions directly affect downstream drinking water, fisheries, recreation economies, and public health — especially for rural and environmental justice communities. Limiting review shifts risk from project developers to residents and local governments.

EPA should withdraw the proposal and preserve a broad interpretation of Section 401 that allows meaningful review of entire projects and protects downstream waters, springs, and communities.

Respectfully submitted.

Cliff Thaell, Vice Chair, Sierra Club Florida Chapter

As a public health professional, I know how crucial it is for our policies to stress prevention and the precautionary principle. There is enormous evidence that your deregulatory approach will bring avoidable illness, suffering, and death. In addition, the damage to health will result in damage to the economy. 

To Administrator Zeldin,

I'm appalled at the EPA plan to undermine Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (CWA). I very strongly oppose the changes that the EPA now proposes. 

Under the Clean Water Act, states and tribes have a vital tool to help protect water quality fir their people. Your proposed changes to Section 401 would recklessly limit that scope. Those changes would block regulators from looking beyond the pollution discharged into waterways to evaluate the overall water quality impact of a project. 

States and authorized Tribes must be enabled to determine the scope of review needed to protect water quality. They must not be restricted to a shrunken range of federally-protected waters and permitted only to examine direct effects of discharges into those waters. 

The broader water-quality effects caused by a project as a whole are what communities rely on the Clean Water Act to analyze and mitigate.

Far beyond the spot where discharge occurs, water quality can be damaged. Limiting the scope of any Section 401 analysis would block crucial reviews of the impacts upstream and downstream of planned projects. 

Under the changes that the EPA has proposed, states and Tribes could lose their ability to use Section 401 to protect many smaller streams, wetlands and headwaters. That would leave state and tribal decision-makers unable to block, or put conditions on, federally permitted projects that could damage those waters -- even if those conditions are vital to the safety of local drinking water supplies, recreation, flood control, or fisheries.

Restricting the scope and timeline of analyses would undermine the CWA's goal of ensuring that states, territories, and Tribes are enabled to protect their water resources. It would instead only benefit the corporations advancing project proposals. Taxpayers would wind up burdened by the costs of added cleanup of pollution that couldn't be mitigated because it didn't get analyzed due to the discharge only constraints. Such a restriction would mean approvals for dangerous projects that should not be permitted. Absent proper review, regulators and the public would very sadly fail to learn of harmful impacts and risks that would, under existing policies, be revealed during analyses that we currently benefit from.

comment_text:
I write to strongly oppose the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed rule to again
improperly weaken regulations related to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (CWA or the Act). Section
401 represents an important tool used by states and Tribes to protect state and Tribal water resources
from the impacts of federally permitted development. Section 401 is a linchpin of the cooperative
federalism structure envisioned by Congress when it passed the Act in 1972 and is specifically designed
to empower states and Tribes. The proposed rule would dramatically undercut the role provided to
states and Tribes by the Act in protecting their waters.
 
The proposed rule largely recycles a rule issued in 2020 that upended almost fifty years of strong state
and Tribal authority to ensure that projects such as dams, pipelines, highways, datacenters, and other
projects are protective of state and Tribal waters and the important services they provide people and
communities. The harm done by the 2020 rule was substantially corrected in 2023 by a revised rule that
restored the proper role for states and Tribes envisioned by the Act and the long-standing regulatory
structure that stood in place since 1971. In doing so, it also updated the rule to clarify that state and
Tribal reviews were appropriately limited to water related requirements and that there was a clear and
timely process for applicants to follow.
 
The proposed rule is an unnecessary retread of the rejected 2020 rule. Of foremost
concern, it would violate the Act by rejecting its clear meaning and overturning Supreme Court
precedent confirming that meaning by limiting the scope of certification from the activity as a whole to
the “discharge from a point source” of a project. This would dramatically limit the ability of states and
Tribes to look at the totality of potential impacts and harms to waters from a project. For instance, it
could eliminate or undermine state and Tribes from being able to put in place protective measures so
that rivers and streams have adequate flow, habitat is protected, and designated uses like fishing and
recreation enjoyed by the public are not disturbed or destroyed.
It is hard to see this proposal as anything thing other than an unwarranted assault on clean water and
state and Tribal rights. Any concerns, which we feel were misplaced at the time, about uncertainty
around timing or process were addressed with the changes in the 2023 rule. The 2023 rule also makes it
clear that certification, conditions, and denial must regard water quality requirements. The
 combined result of these two proposed rules will be far fewer opportunities for state and Tribes to
protect their waters under Section 401 and far weaker options for them to do so in the limited number
of times it is triggered. This will lead to more water pollution, more destruction of critical aquatic
resources, more risk of flooding and other disasters, more threats to drinking water and public health,
the loss of habitat, deprivation of recreational and other opportunities, and other negative
consequences for our waters and the people – which is all of us – that rely on them.
We strongly urge you not to move forward with this ill-conceived and unnecessary rule and keep the
existing 2023 rule in place.
Sincerely,
Marie Noel

comment_text:
For more than fifty years, Section 401 of the Clean Water Act has given states and Tribes real power to protect their water. It allows them to review major federal projects like pipelines, dams, mines, and power plants before permits are issued. When projects threaten drinking water, wetlands, or fisheries, communities can step in and demand changes or stop them outright.

This rule strips states and Tribes of meaningful review power, forces decisions through on an industry timetable, and clears obstacles for polluters that communities spent decades building.

Section 401 has been used to block or reshape fossil fuel pipelines, mining operations, and industrial facilities that would have contaminated water supplies or destroyed ecosystems. Weakening it hands the advantage to corporations that see clean water protections as a barrier to profit.

Frontline communities will now pay the price. Tribes lose one of the only tools they have to defend sacred waters and cultural sites. Rural towns like mine lose leverage to protect wells and rivers. Downstream communities are left dealing with contamination while corporations walk away with the profits.

Industry supporters openly praise this proposal because it makes pollution cheaper. Shorter reviews mean less scrutiny. Narrower standards mean fewer protections. Corporations get certainty and speed, while communities absorb the health risks, cleanup costs, and long-term damage.

This fight is about who controls our water. Local governments and Tribes understand their waterways, their ecosystems, and their people. Corporate lobbyists in Washington understand balance sheets. Section 401 has always been about keeping those priorities straight.

This proposal did not come out of nowhere. Pipeline companies, energy developers, data center operators, and industrial polluters have spent years lobbying to narrow Section 401. They want faster approvals, fewer conditions, and fewer chances for states or Tribes to say no.

We must not allow corporate polluters to rewrite clean water protections.

I oppose the proposed revisions to the 401 Rule of Clean Water Act. Clean Water Act protections are widely supported by Americans. The 401 rule requires careful checks on potential impacts to streams and rivers, providing an important safeguard to clean water resources, as we continue the important work of infrastructure, energy, and other projects that benefit Americans. These are rivers and streams where we cool off in the summer, where children play, where families fish, and which contribute to our drinking water. It is far more economical to protect these waterways from pollution than to clean them up and restore them. 

In particular, the narrowing of scope to only point source discharges does not adequately protect waters. Point source discharges are not the only impacts that degrade waterways. Reviewing agencies need the flexibility to consider full project impacts on clean water. 

The timelines in the rule should maintain flexibility for unforeseen circumstances, even while the federal, state, and Tribal governments seek to move projects efficiently through regulatory reviews.

comment_text:
I write to strongly oppose the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed rule to again improperly weaken regulations related to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act (CWA or the Act). Section 401 represents an important tool used by states and Tribes to protect state and Tribal water resources from the impacts of federally permitted development. Section 401 is a linchpin of the cooperative federalism structure envisioned by Congress when it passed the Act in 1972 and is specifically designed to empower states and Tribes. The proposed rule would dramatically undercut the role provided to states and Tribes by the Act in protecting their waters.
 
The proposed rule largely recycles a rule issued in 2020 that upended almost fifty years of strong state and Tribal authority to ensure that projects such as dams, pipelines, highways, datacenters, and other projects are protective of state and Tribal waters and the important services they provide people and communities. The harm done by the 2020 rule was substantially corrected in 2023 by a revised rule that restored the proper role for states and Tribes envisioned by the Act and the long-standing regulatory structure that stood in place since 1971. In doing so, it also updated the rule to clarify that state and Tribal reviews were appropriately limited to water related requirements and that there was a clear and timely process for applicants to follow.
 
The proposed rule is by and large an unnecessary retread of the rejected 2020 rule. Of foremost concern, it would violate the Act by rejecting its clear meaning and overturning Supreme Court precedent confirming that meaning by limiting the scope of certification from the activity as a whole to the “discharge from a point source” of a project. This would dramatically limit the ability of states and Tribes to look at the totality of potential impacts and harms to waters from a project. For instance, it could eliminate or undermine state and Tribes from being able to put in place protective measures so that rivers and streams have adequate flow, habitat is protected, and designated uses like fishing and recreation enjoyed by the public are not disturbed or destroyed.

It is hard to see this proposal as anything thing other than an unwarranted assault on clean water and state and Tribal rights. Any concerns, which we feel were misplaced at the time, about uncertainty around timing or process were addressed with the changes in the 2023 rule. The 2023 rule also makes it clear that certification, conditions, and denial must regard water quality requirements. Moreover, the Section 401 process rarely results in the denial or undue delay of projects. For example, as EPA’s Economic Analysis shows, almost all permits issued by the Corps (which make up the overwhelming number of permits subject to Section 401) are either granted (95.5%) or waived (3.8%). Only 0.8% are denied.[JD2] 
As such, this proposed rule is not seeking to address any plausible problem. It also must be seen in relation to recent changes to the scope of Clean Water Act protections generally. Section 401 is only triggered when a federal permit or license involving a discharge to “waters of the United States” is at issue. In fact, most federal permits and licenses that trigger Section 401 are Section 404 discharge permits under the Clean Water Act itself. In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court issued a decision in Sackett v. sEPA that dramatically reduced the number of waters covered by the federal Clean Water Act. Subsequently, this EPA is finalizing a rule that would even further limit the number of waters protected by the Act. If the proposed EPA rule governing “waters of the United States” is issued as proposed, it would result in an estimated 81% of historically federally protected wetlands lacking Clean Water Act protection[JD3] . Massive losses in protections under the Act for streams is also at issue. With these rollbacks, many projects will no longer need CWA permits, meaning that the trigger for Section 401 review for many projects will disappear altogether. 
The combined result of these two proposed rules will be far fewer opportunities for state and Tribes to protect their waters under Section 401 and far weaker options for them to do so in the limited number of times it is triggered. This will lead to more water pollution, more destruction of critical aquatic resources, more risk of flooding and other disasters, more threats to drinking water and public health, the loss of habitat, deprivation of recreational and other opportunities, and other negative consequences for our waters and the people – which is all of us – that rely on them.
I strongly urge you not to move forward with this ill-conceived and unnecessary rule and keep the existing 2023 rule in place.

comment_text:
I appreciate the opportunity to communicate my strong opposition to the EPA’s proposed 2026 rule changes that would circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water.

I have a personal stake in this bill as I have spent years as a scout master teaching the youth values of land and water stewardship, something this bill is indirect opposition to. I am born and raised in Minnesota and I’ve seen how important our clean water is to everyone here. It is at the center of our tourism, and is a critical part of the culture. I have brought hundreds of kids upstate to experience the wonders of the boundary waters in trips that have taught them values of hard work, perseverance, and responsibility. These lands are so critical to so many young people‘s journeys and this bill would destroy these natural wonders.

The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. 

The EPA’s proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. The EPA’s proposed 2026 certification rules are unlawful, unreasonable, and just plain wrong. Specifically:

1.) I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations.

2.) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park.

3.) I oppose all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water.

4.) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 

5.) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? 

The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish. These activities are not just for fun, there are how we survive and central to our tourism industry that brings in millions of dollars a year. Not only with these social repercussions be huge, the economic ones would be devastating long term. 

Thank you for considering my comments,

I appreciate the opportunity to communicate my strong opposition to the EPA’s proposed 2026 rule changes that would circumscribe certification authority used by States and Tribes to protect clean water.

The Clean Water Act was adopted by Congress to restore and maintain clean water and to ensure that States and Tribes could prevent violation of the water quality requirements they have adopted. 

The EPA’s proposed certification rules would serve the special interests of polluters at the expense of clean water, the rights of States to protect the health and welfare of their residents, and the sovereignty of Tribes. The EPA’s proposed 2026 certification rules are unlawful, unreasonable, and just plain wrong. Specifically:

1.) I oppose the Rule’s elimination of current regulations facilitating Tribal certification authority and supporting neighboring/downstream Tribes in objecting to federal permits and preventing violations of Reservation water quality requirements. Shame on you for erasing Tribes from these regulations.

2.) I oppose the Rule’s restrictions that would prevent any State or Tribe in the United States from setting conditions on Federal “general permits.” In Minnesota, we’ve used existing certification authority to prevent degradation and protect streams, Exceptional Aquatic Life Use waters, and Outstanding Resource Value waters, like the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and Voyageurs National Park.

3.) I oppose all the Rule’s changes that tighten a noose around the scope of certification. They would prevent conditions or denial of Federal permits even if activities would violate State and Tribal standards and contaminate lakes and streams due to wetlands destruction, waste stockpiling, or seepage through groundwater into surface water.

4.) I oppose the Rule’s forced waiver of State or Tribal certification after a year even if time is needed due to public process, acts of God, or because the project proposer concealed the truth about water impacts in its draft permit application. This rule would encourage polluters to hide the facts and do a bait-and-switch after time has run out for certification. 

5.) I oppose the Rule’s creation of new power in the EPA Administrator to determine without guardrails that an entire category of discharges will never affect downstream States or Tribes and deprive them of authority to object to violations of water quality requirements. What category would this EPA remove from certification review? All pipeline discharge? All mining waste? 

The EPA must reject or withdraw its 2026 proposed rule to undermine State and Tribal certification. Existing rules under the Clean Water Act do a much better job of protecting us and our children from contaminated water that they can’t safely drink, swim in, or fish.

Thank you for considering my comments,

Happy Monday!

Water pollution has serious impacts, and any decision that threatens to increase pollution and harm public health needs to be analyzed and weighed. Waterways are not solely impacted in the spot where discharge occurs and limiting the scope of the Section 401 analysis would result in a lack of review of project impacts upstream and downstream. 

With the changes proposed, states and Tribes could lose the ability to use Section 401 to protect local drinking water supplies, fisheries, and waters for recreation as the discharge only reporting prevents proper analysis lf proposed projects.

I urge you to strengthen the Clean Water Act and protect drinking water, public health, and species habitat in waterways and wetlands. 

With gratitude,
Donovan Barnes

comment_text:
The new rule, as proposed, would limit the abilities of states and tribes to review and consider broader water-quality effects caused by proposed projects when weighing certification. This would weaken the abilities of potentially affected parties and stakeholders to provide oversight of projects that may have water-quality effects not limited strictly to discharge.

The proposed rule would prevent states from protecting vital water resources such as smaller streams, wetlands and headwaters within their borders, leaving state regulators powerless to block, or place conditions on, federally permitted projects that could damage those waters, even if they are vital to local drinking water supplies, fisheries, recreation or flood control.

The new rule seeks to subvert the intent of the Clean Water Act by relying on overly strict definitions to remove the ability of states and tribes to steward water resources in the face of federally permitted projects. At a time when the Southwest is in the worst drought in over 1200 years, this is no time to roll back protections and tie the hands of the governments closest to, and most reliant on, these increasingly scarce and therefore valuable resources.

Please maintain the current rule as-is.

I am submitting these comments to address the proposed rule from the Environmental Protection Agency entitled Updating the Water Quality Certification Regulations (40 CFR Part 121). The proposed rule aims to update various substantive and procedural aspects of Clean Water Act Section 401 water quality certification in response to concerns over the 2023 Rule.
However, it is also important that any changes to the law respect the principles of cooperative federalism that are embodied in the Clean Water Act. Section 401 of the Act plays an important role in giving States and authorized Tribes an important role in protecting the quality of water within their jurisdictions. Any modifications should ensure that they retain this ability.
I urge EPA to continue its dialogue with States, Tribes, and industry representatives, as well as the public, to ensure that the final rule finds an appropriate balance between clarity, environmental protection, and administrative efficiency, as set forth in the statutory intent of Section 401.

comment_text:
We must maintain the progress made with the Clean Water Act that has cleared our rivers of deadly poisons, allowed fish and marine life populations to thrive, provided for safe drinking water for communities and cities, given back to wildlife water to drink and maintain their lives with. Only with The Clean Water Act has this been possible. 

This comment particularly concerns a proposal by the EPA to revise Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. The attempt to is disallow states, communities and tribes their right to protect themselves and their environments, water supplies and wildlife, from the devastation that some federally permitted projects inevitably bring to the places people live, work, raise families and have productive lives. 

Trying to eliminate states rights over federal overreach is a fundamental issue the Constitution addresses amply, purposefully preventing this. This idea that whatever the federal government says should be built regardless of the harm to citizens and environments of individual states and their communities, or to Tribes and their sovereign lands, is a states rights issue. 
Then to mock the mandate of the EPA by making it an agency of destroying environment, public health and safe water, soil to grown food, air quality, operating completely illegally, is a threat to all Americans, their families, and way of life. I am writing to urge EPA to withdraw its proposed revisions to Section 401 of the Clean Water Act. I believe this proposal would drastically limit the ability of states and Tribal governments to protect water quality.

Federally permitted projects can threaten drinking water, fisheries, and public health if proper safeguards are not in place.

Section 401 embodies cooperative federalism and ensures that local expertise and community voices are not overridden by federal permitting decisions. Weakening this authority would disproportionately harm frontline and underserved communities and make it harder to prevent pollution before it occurs.

The proposed rule undermines decades of effective clean water protections and prioritizes industry convenience over the public interest. I urge EPA to reject this proposal and fully uphold Section 401 as Congress intended.

Thank you.

comment_text: This comment is regarding Docket ID # EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929. I strongly oppose the changes to the Clean Water Act certification regulations being proposed by the EPA that will weaken local entities' ability to preserve and protect their natural resources. I live in Northern Minnesota, where multinational corporations are eager to reap short term profits from our priceless resources without regard to the long term impact on our human and natural communities. It is essential that States and Tribes retain the ability to control potentially harmful and disruptive corporate activity in the communities they represent. States and Tribes across the United States rely on certification to protect clean water from contamination resulting from inadequate, politically-motivated, or reckless federal permitting of facilities and activities. Certification is an important guardrail to ensure that Federal action and corporate polluters do not pollute streams, lakes, rivers, and wetlands in complete disregard for State and Tribal water quality requirements. Please do not gut the intentions of the Clean Water Act, which has been so imperative in the protection and improvement of our environment. Thank you!

comment_text:
To Whom it may concern in regards to Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929:

I am a resident of Park County Montana, I live just north of Yellowstone National Park as well as the Absaroka Beartooth Wilderness. The Yellowstone River flows through Park County and my town of Livingston, Montana. The Yellowstone River and the many tributaries that feed it are a life source for my community. These waters (including groundwater and seasonal wetlands) supports the habitat of wildlife and plant species that I care about and recreate in. Having an intact ecosystem is important to me. These waters support local agriculture and a tourism economy that helps my community to thrive.

Statutory requirement 401(a)(1) requires meaningful opportunity for public comment. Codifying a comment period of no more than 30 days for EPA certifications (40 CFR 121.17(a)) contradicts 401(a)(1). 30 days is insufficient for meaningful review, analysis, and response for complex projects and/or associated technical documents. This is particularly true in rural and tribal communities where capacity for stakeholders to provide substantiative comments is limited by time and resources. 

I oppose codifying a comment period of no more than 30 days for EPA certifications. The EPA should retain flexibility to extend the period for public comment based on project complexity.

Limiting the scope of Section 401 certifications to “discharges” vs “activities” ignores non-point source pollution and does not consider the entire hydrology of the system in which the certification pertains to, such as construction runoff, erosion, impervious surfaces and sediment transport. 

For example: I reside less than 1/4 of a mile of a rail yard that is an active superfund cleanup following decades of contamination. As proposed in these changes, our aquifer would not be reviewable and my communities health would be compromised.

I oppose the proposed EPA change to define “discharge” for purposes of CWA section 401, at 40 CFR 121.1(c), as “a discharge from a point source into waters of the United States.” Contaminants in upstream, intermittent streams and wetlands directly impacts downstream water quality and drinking water. The proposed changes compromise the health and wellbeing of all by compromising water quality. 

Thank you for considering my comments,
Melissa Stringham Frady

This comment is in reference to Docket ID # EPA-HQ-OW-2025-2929.
Deregulation of current water quality regulations will have serious and lasting effects. Residents of northern Minnesota, like me, highly value clean water and lakes and are very concerned that protections stay in force.
